“Are you?”

“Then I’m Claire.”

“Only when I’m distracted,” he said.

“By what?”

He looked at her rather than answering.

When she finished her drink, he didn’t assume.

“Would you like another?”

“No.”

“Should I go?”

Mara set down her glass. “You could ask me something else.”

He took a breath. “Would you like to come upstairs with me?”

“Yes,” she said, and enjoyed how quickly his composure slipped.

In the elevator, he stood beside her with his hands in his pockets.

“You’re awfully quiet now,” she said.

“I used most of my good material downstairs.”

“That’s unfortunate. I was promised a charming stranger.”

“No promises were made.”

She caught his sleeve and drew him closer. “Then I’ll have to take my chances.”

At the room, he fumbled the key card.

“First time doing this?” she asked.

“With you? Apparently.”

That broke them both. He leaned his forehead against hers, laughing softly, until she touched his cheek.

“Hello, Daniel.”

His smile settled. “Hello, Claire.”

This kiss was slower than their habitual greetings, tentative for a moment before she pulled him nearer. Inside, he stopped just long enough to ask, “Still having fun?”

“Very much.”

She slipped the key card from his hand and placed it on the table.

“Stay a while,” she told the stranger who knew her best.

He closed the door.

For their tenth anniversary, Daniel made the meal he had ruined on their third date.

“You’re a brave man,” Lena said, surveying the candles.

“I’ve learned things in ten years.”

“About cooking?”

“Mostly about ordering backup.”

She laughed, and he felt the same foolish relief he had felt a decade ago: she was here; she was happy to see him.

The table stood beside the open window, laid with their wedding china and the linen napkins they always decided were too nice to use. Outside, rain whispered against the fire escape. Inside, garlic browned in butter, and the record player worked its way through an old jazz album.

This time, the meal was perfect.

Lena took three bites before setting down her fork.

“Well?” he asked.

“I’m trying to think of something cutting to say.”

“Take your time.”

She reached across the table instead. He gave her his hand.

They talked until the candles burned low: about the apartment with the crooked floors, the disastrous camping trip, the morning they had brought their dog home in a laundry basket. Then Daniel admitted that he had kept the grocery list from their first dinner together.

“No, you haven’t.”

He fetched it from the sideboard.

There it was, folded small, with *ask if she likes olives* written beneath the pasta.

Lena pressed her fingertips to her mouth.

“I was nervous,” he said.

“You asked me about olives twice.”

“I wanted to get something right.”

She stood and came around the table. When she kissed him, he caught her gently by the waist.

“You did,” she whispered.

For a while, neither of them moved.

Then Lena glanced at the dishes. “We should clear these.”

“Very romantic.”

“I have plans for the table.”

His smile changed.

Together they moved the plates to the sideboard, laughing when their hands collided over the bread basket. Daniel put out the nearest candles and checked that the old table didn’t wobble before helping her onto its edge.

“Still practical,” she said.

“Ten years of marriage.”

She drew him close by his loosened tie. He kissed her slowly this time, with no timer about to ring, no restaurant closing around them, no reason to stop and ask for the bill.

The rain thickened beyond the window. Lena’s heels slipped to the floor.

“Happy anniversary,” he murmured against her cheek.

She rested her forehead against his, smiling.

“Stay right here.”

And he did, as the record played on and the candlelight softened around them.

She laughed because he remembered.

Inside, she switched on the bedside lamp. They sat together on the edge of the bed, close enough that their knees touched, and took a moment simply to look at each other.

“And?”

His free hand settles at your waist, tentative despite the strength in it. You step closer, answering the question he has not quite asked.

You answer aloud, so there can be no uncertainty. “Yes.”

“Not unless I’ve been incredibly obvious.”

“You offered to help him move.”

You and Lena have talked before about inviting someone into your relationship—not as a repair, not as a test, but as something you might both enjoy. Neither is the way you watch his hands.

Lena reaches across the table. “We can ask. He can say no. So can we.”

The conversation is less elegant than you imagined.

Adrian’s expression softens.

“Still yes?” Lena asks.

For a moment, neither of you moves.

The hotel door stands open between you, and after a year of imagining this meeting, you can think only that your lover’s coat is wet. Rain beads on the dark wool. One drop clings absurdly to the end of a sleeve.

“You’re here,” you say.

“Yes.”

Their voice is different without a speaker between you. Quieter. Close enough that you don’t have to listen for it.

You reach for their hand.

Cold fingers, familiar knuckles. You rub your thumb over the small scar you remember, and they look down at the gesture. Their breath catches in a way that undoes your careful welcome.

Then you are holding each other.

The coat is damp against your cheek. Beneath the rain you recognize their soap, and you press closer, eyes shut, while their palm settles against the back of your head.

“I missed this,” they murmur.

You nod against their shoulder. You cannot yet manage the past tense.

Inside, the room is warm. Amber lamplight falls across rumpled curtains; beyond the window, tires whisper over the wet Paris street. Somewhere downstairs, crockery clatters, followed by laughter.

You help them out of their coat. They touch your cheek with the backs of their fingers, almost tentatively.

“Still all right?”

You turn your face into their hand. “Come here.”

The first kiss is brief. Afterward, you remain forehead to forehead, smiling with an awkwardness neither of you expected. Their thumb brushes away a tear before you realize you have cried.

There is time now. Time to kiss again, to sit together at the edge of the bed, to discover that their hand still fits into yours without adjustment. You tell them something foolish about the journey. They laugh, and the last tight, watchful part of you begins to loosen.

When you switch off the lamp, you leave the curtains open. The city casts a pale rectangle across the ceiling.

Later, beneath the cool linen, you wake enough to feel an arm resting around your waist. You lay your hand over it.

This time, when you reach across the bed, there is someone there.

Across from him, Bell stopped smiling.

The piano player lifted his fingers from the keys. Behind the bar, Hettie eased a bottle onto the shelf without letting the glass touch wood.

Rusk kept his palm where it was. “I rode into that express car.”

“And I got you out.”

“You got yourself out. I happened to be behind you.”

Bell’s chair creaked. His right hand disappeared beneath the table.

Rusk shoved back hard enough to tip his own chair. The knife came up where his belly had been, striking a brass button and flicking it across the room. Before Bell could draw back, Rusk caught his wrist with both hands.

For a moment they stood bent over the table, shaking with effort. Bell was shorter, but he had a miner’s shoulders. He drove forward. The table skidded, its legs screeching over the floorboards, and the bag toppled between their boots.

Rusk tried to turn the knife toward the wall.

Bell stamped on his instep.

Pain loosened Rusk’s grip. The blade dragged across the outside of his forearm—a quick pressure, followed by a hot sting that spread almost to his elbow. He saw the slit in his sleeve before he understood he had been cut.

Then the cloth began to darken.

He slammed his forehead into Bell’s face.

Bell staggered without letting go of the knife. His free hand flew to his nose, and his breath came through his mouth in a wet, startled gasp.

Rusk seized the nearest chair and thrust it legs-first between them.

The knife struck a rung. Bell yanked it free and lunged again, but Rusk drove the chair forward, pinning him against the bar. Bottles rattled. Bell’s boots scrabbled for purchase.

Neither man moved.

Rusk’s injured arm had begun to throb. Blood ran beneath his cuff and gathered against his palm, making the chair back slippery. He shifted his weight, trying not to show how badly his foot hurt.

Hettie stepped around the bar with a shotgun.

Rusk eased the chair back. Bell folded over, coughing, one hand braced on his knee. Blood dripped from his nose onto the sawdust.

Nobody reached for them.

The precinct had one working light, and it was losing an argument with the dark.

Detective Voss stood beneath it with his sleeves rolled up. Detective Keene sat backward in a chair by the door, smoking something that smelled like wet cardboard and somebody else’s bad luck.

On the desk lay my wallet, my license, and a photograph of a girl they kept calling a runaway.

Voss picked up the phone book.

“You know what your problem is, Mercer?”

“I never learned to enjoy police hospitality.”

He hit me across the ribs.

The chair scraped sideways. For a second there wasn’t any room in my chest for air. I stared at a brown stain on the linoleum and waited for the floor to settle.

Voss set the book down neatly.

“No marks,” he said.

I’d heard that one before. Cops believed all kinds of things when believing made the paperwork easier.

Keene blew smoke toward the ceiling. It stayed around us. Cheap tobacco had soaked into his tie, the curtains, the damp wool of the coat hanging behind me. I could taste it when I finally got a breath.

“Let’s start again,” he said. “Who hired you?”

“A woman with forty dollars.”

“Name.”

“She wanted that kept private.”

Voss reached for the book.

“Funny profession,” Keene said. “Private investigator. Makes a man think certain things belong to him.”

“They do. Until a cop empties his pockets.”

Voss hit me again.

This time I saw it coming. That didn’t improve it. Pain spread under my ribs, deep and sickening, and my hands closed around the arms of the chair. One of my fingernails caught a splinter. I concentrated on that. It was a small hurt I could understand.

Keene leaned forward.

“You were at the Marlow Hotel last night.”

“Terrible service.”

“You talked to Evelyn Shaw.”

“She had complaints too.”

“Where is she?”

I looked at the photograph on the desk. Evelyn at seventeen, standing beside a bicycle, squinting into summer. The woman I’d met at the Marlow had been twenty-three and so frightened she’d asked me to check the corridor twice.

She’d shown me a ledger. Names, dates, payments. I’d recognized Keene’s signature before I recognized his face.

“Maybe she ran away,” I said. “That’s what you boys put in the report.”

Voss’s jaw shifted. Keene stopped rocking his chair.

Outside, a typewriter rattled. Someone laughed. It bothered me more than the phone book, that laugh. Whoever it was would go home later and say it had been a quiet night.

Keene dropped his cigarette and ground it out.

“You think you’re protecting her?”

“No.”

“Then what are you doing?”

“Making you work.”

Voss lifted the book, but Keene caught his wrist.

For a moment neither of them moved. Then Voss lowered it. He looked disappointed in a tired, practical way, like a man told to put away a tool before the job was finished.

Keene came close enough for me to see the shaving cut beneath his ear.

“Listen carefully. You’re going to tell us where she is. Then you’re going to sign a statement saying she tried to sell you stolen city records.”

“And afterward?”

“You walk out.”

I looked at my hat on the filing cabinet. Voss had put it there when they brought me in, brim up, almost considerate.

“My office knows I’m here,” I said.

“You haven’t got a secretary.”

“No. Just a landlord who gets interested when I miss rent.”

Keene watched me. I let him. Breathing hurt, but I kept it shallow and regular.

At last he stepped back.

“Give him a minute.”

They went out together. Voss took the phone book.

The door shut, and I sat with the tobacco stink and the photograph. My ribs hurt worse now that nobody was hitting them. I wanted a cigarette, which seemed like poor judgment even by my standards.

From the hall came the low murmur of their voices, then the scrape of a match.

They hadn’t asked about the ledger yet.

I held on to that.

The precinct had one working light, and it was losing an argument with the dark.

Detective Voss stood beneath it with his sleeves rolled up. Detective Keene sat backward in a chair by the door, smoking something that smelled like wet cardboard and somebody else’s bad luck.

On the desk lay my wallet, my license, and a photograph of a girl they kept calling a runaway.

Voss picked up the phone book.

“You know what your problem is, Mercer?”

“I never learned to enjoy police hospitality.”

He hit me across the ribs.

The chair scraped sideways. For a second there wasn’t any room in my chest for air. I stared at a brown stain on the linoleum and waited for the floor to settle.

Voss set the book down neatly.

“No marks,” he said.

I’d heard that one before. Cops believed all kinds of things when believing made the paperwork easier.

Keene blew smoke toward the ceiling. It stayed around us. Cheap tobacco had soaked into his tie, the curtains, the damp wool of the coat hanging behind me. I could taste it when I finally got a breath.

“Let’s start again,” he said. “Who hired you?”

“A woman with forty dollars.”

“Name.”

“She wanted that kept private.”

Voss reached for the book.

“Funny profession,” Keene said. “Private investigator. Makes a man think certain things belong to him.”

“They do. Until a cop empties his pockets.”

Voss hit me again.

This time I saw it coming. That didn’t improve it. Pain spread under my ribs, deep and sickening, and my hands closed around the arms of the chair. One of my fingernails caught a splinter. I concentrated on that. It was a small hurt I could understand.

Keene leaned forward.

“You were at the Marlow Hotel last night.”

“Terrible service.”

“You talked to Evelyn Shaw.”

“She had complaints too.”

“Where is she?”

I looked at the photograph on the desk. Evelyn at seventeen, standing beside a bicycle, squinting into summer. The woman I’d met at the Marlow had been twenty-three and so frightened she’d asked me to check the corridor twice.

She’d shown me a ledger. Names, dates, payments. I’d recognized Keene’s signature before I recognized his face.

“Maybe she ran away,” I said. “That’s what you boys put in the report.”

Voss’s jaw shifted. Keene stopped rocking his chair.

Outside, a typewriter rattled. Someone laughed. It bothered me more than the phone book, that laugh. Whoever it was would go home later and say it had been a quiet night.

Keene dropped his cigarette and ground it out.

“You think you’re protecting her?”

“No.”

“Then what are you doing?”

“Making you work.”

Voss lifted the book, but Keene caught his wrist.

For a moment neither of them moved. Then Voss lowered it. He looked disappointed in a tired, practical way, like a man told to put away a tool before the job was finished.

Keene came close enough for me to see the shaving cut beneath his ear.

“Listen carefully. You’re going to tell us where she is. Then you’re going to sign a statement saying she tried to sell you stolen city records.”

“And afterward?”

“You walk out.”

I looked at my hat on the filing cabinet. Voss had put it there when they brought me in, brim up, almost considerate.

“My office knows I’m here,” I said.

“You haven’t got a secretary.”

“No. Just a landlord who gets interested when I miss rent.”

Keene watched me. I let him. Breathing hurt, but I kept it shallow and regular.

At last he stepped back.

“Give him a minute.”

They went out together. Voss took the phone book.

The door shut, and I sat with the tobacco stink and the photograph. My ribs hurt worse now that nobody was hitting them. I wanted a cigarette, which seemed like poor judgment even by my standards.

From the hall came the low murmur of their voices, then the scrape of a match.

They hadn’t asked about the ledger yet.

I held on to that.

results.model_response:
The closet smelled of cedar and the coat her father wore to funerals.

Mara had backed into it without turning on the light. Now a wire hanger pressed against her cheek, and beneath her bare foot lay something small and sharp—a belt buckle, maybe. She couldn’t shift her weight to find out.

Downstairs, a drawer slid open.

Shut.

Another opened.

“Not here,” the man said.

He wasn’t calling to anyone. His voice had the distracted irritation of someone looking for spare batteries.

Mara held her phone against her stomach. The emergency call had failed twice. One bar appeared, vanished, appeared again. She had silenced it, dimmed the screen, and sent her address to her sister with three words.

*Call the police.*

No reply yet.

A crash came from the kitchen. Pottery scattered across the floor.

“Stupid,” the man muttered. “Don’t rush.”

She heard him walking through the rooms. His pace slowed in the dining room, where the table gave him places to look behind. Then the living room. She knew the long squeak of the floorboard beside the sofa.

Silence.

Mara tried to breathe through her open mouth.

She had seen the gun when he came through the back door. That was what kept returning—not his face, not the broken glass, but how casually he carried it, low beside his leg.

The first stair creaked.

Her phone lit against her fingers.

**Which house? Yours or Dad’s?**

She closed her eyes.

Of course. Her sister would see the address, but she would want to be sure. Dad had been dead only six weeks. They still called it his house.

Mara typed *Dad’s*.

The second stair. The third.

Then the man stopped.

She froze with her thumb hovering above Send.

“Car’s outside,” he said. “Somebody’s here.”

A faint metallic click followed.

“No loose ends. That’s the whole point.”

Mara pressed Send and turned the phone facedown against her stomach.

He resumed climbing.

She remembered leaving a mug on the bedside table. Tea still warm enough to steam. Her shoes beside the bed. Her bag hanging from the chair.

Everything upstairs would tell him where she had been.

At the landing, he paused again.

“Check them all,” he whispered. “Every room. Nobody walks out.”

A door swung inward across the hall.

The little bedroom.

Mara pictured him looking under the narrow bed, pulling back the curtains. She heard the wardrobe handles knock together.

Then the bathroom door struck its rubber stop.

Her leg began to tremble. She pressed her knee into the coats, trying to make the trembling stop before it shook a hanger against the rail.

The footsteps entered her bedroom.

Close now.

A bedspring complained.

He had sat down.

For several seconds, nothing moved. Mara stared into the dark between two hanging sleeves. There was no way to know what he was doing.

Then a soft scrape of ceramic.

He had found the tea.

“Oh,” he said.

The mug clicked back onto the bedside table.

Mara brought one hand over her mouth. She could smell the dust on her fingers.

The bedspring rose.

One step.

Another.

He stopped outside the closet.

At the bottom of the door, the narrow bar of hallway light disappeared beneath his shadow.

Mara’s phone vibrated once against her stomach.

The handle turned.

And the closet door began to creak open.

results.model_response:
By the time Mara saw the river, she was doing a hundred and ten.

It flashed between the warehouses at the end of the avenue, black water carrying the orange scars of dock lights. Somewhere behind her, beyond the howl of engines, a crowd was still cheering. Ten thousand dollars sat in a duffel bag on a stranger’s hood. Her brother’s debt sat in the passenger seat with her, invisible and heavier than any person.

Beside her, the silver coupe edged ahead.

Mara pressed harder.

The engine’s note climbed until it seemed to live inside her teeth. Streetlights strobed across the windshield. Her palms were wet against the wheel, but the rest of her felt wonderfully precise: the twitch of the front tires over patched asphalt, the gear lever warm in her hand, the rival driver’s white knuckles glimpsed through his window.

The coupe drifted close enough to fill her side mirror. She held her line.

At the starting line, tire smoke had rolled through the open windows, bitter and oily. Now that smell clung to the upholstery, mixed with hot metal and the raw gasoline stink of engines pushed too hard. It caught at the back of her throat.

Three blocks to the turn.

The coupe’s brake lights blinked.

Mara waited another heartbeat. That was where she could win: carry more speed, brake later, come out beside him on the final straight.

She moved her foot.

The pedal went down too easily.

For a fraction of a second, she felt only confusion. Her foot had traveled farther than it should. She lifted it and pressed again.

The pedal sank to the floor.

“No.”

The coupe slowed sharply beside her. Then it was behind her, its headlights flooding her mirrors.

Mara pressed harder, bracing against the seat. Nothing caught. No tug against the belt, no dip of the hood. The warehouse at the corner kept rushing toward her at the same impossible speed.

Earlier, a man in a gray jacket had crouched beside her front wheel. She had seen him stand when she came back from handing over her cash.

*Just checking your tire,* he’d said.

She remembered the small tool disappearing into his sleeve.

“Oh, God. You touched it.”

Her voice sounded thin inside the car.

Ahead, floodlights exposed the concrete barriers across the dead end. Red arrows directed racers left through a narrow opening. She could see faces beyond it, spectators leaning over the fence with phones raised.

Mara hit the horn and held it.

One face turned. Then another. A phone dropped.

She tried to scrub speed without wrenching the car sideways, arms rigid, eyes searching for space. The turn came at her too fast. She caught a flash of the silver coupe slipping safely left, its rear tires smoking, and then there was only the barrier.

Her right foot was still crushing the useless pedal.

She let go of the horn. Both hands closed around the wheel.

The impact folded the hood upward with a sound so violent she felt it before she heard it. The belt seized her chest. An airbag burst into her face, hot and chemical. Glass sprayed through the cabin.

The car struck at an angle, climbed the broken edge of the barrier, and tipped.

For an instant, Mara saw the road through the passenger window. Sparks streamed beneath her, bright enough to light the empty seat. Then the roof hit, and the windshield whitened into a thousand cracks.

Metal dragged over asphalt. Something heavy tore loose. The car rolled once more and landed hard on its wheels.

Silence lasted less than a second.

The horn began again, stuck in a flat, senseless cry.

Mara tried to breathe and couldn’t get enough air. Her chest hurt. Dust from the airbag floated in the dashboard light, and somewhere close, a liquid was dripping steadily.

The smell of gasoline grew stronger.

She pulled at the belt latch. Missed it. Tried again with fingers she could barely feel.

Outside, people were shouting to get back. Someone else was shouting for an extinguisher.

Mara found the latch and pressed.

Behind the buckled hood, a small orange flame appeared.

results.model_response:
The hotel had placed a card beside the bed assuring him that every surface had been cleaned to the highest standard. He moved it beneath the rifle’s receiver to protect the desk from oil.

On television, a woman stood outside a government building in the rain.

“—survived by his wife and two daughters.”

He reduced the volume. He preferred the captions, though their mistakes irritated him.

The rifle lay across a folded bath towel, its bolt assembly separate from the receiver. Under the desk lamp, the locking lugs cast small, exact shadows. He examined the extractor through his glasses, then made a notation in a pocket ledger. A faint mark on the stock had been there for months. He knew its shape well enough to recognize it without looking closely.

The television changed to a photograph of the dead man at a beach. One daughter rode on his shoulders. The other was caught mid-stride at the edge of the frame, her face blurred by movement.

The photograph told him nothing useful.

His client’s documents had called the man *the subject*. The news called him *a devoted father*. Neither description had entered into the agreement.

He turned the rifle slightly beneath the lamp. The trigger housing showed ordinary wear. He recorded that, too. His handwriting was small and legible, with none of the abbreviations he used when making notes for himself. The ledger might eventually have to be understood by someone else.

A correspondent began describing the killing as senseless.

He glanced up.

That was a word people used when they had not been given the relevant information. There had been a request, a price, an acceptance, and a result. He knew nothing of the client’s ultimate purpose. Finding out was neither necessary nor covered by his fee.

His phone vibrated beside the empty coffee cup.

**Confirmation received. Balance released.**

He checked the amount. Correct.

On the screen, a colleague of the dead man struggled through a statement. She kept looking down at a page that was becoming wet in the rain. He watched her lose her place, recover it, then abandon the page altogether.

The captions continued after she stopped speaking.

He returned his attention to the rifle. There were limits to what he could inspect properly in a hotel room. He noted the work to be done later and closed the ledger.

The agreement was now fulfilled. The phrase he would use, if asked, was *contractual obligation*. He had used it once with an intermediary who seemed to expect some expression of enthusiasm. It had ended that part of the conversation.

He felt no need to use it aloud here.

A knock came at the door.

He covered the desk with the second towel before answering.

A room-service waiter stood beside a trolley. Young, tired, a shaving cut just beneath his jaw.

“Club sandwich?”

“Yes.”

“Where would you like it?”

“By the window.”

The waiter set out the plate and lifted the silver cover. He glanced at the television.

“Awful thing,” he said.

The man signed the receipt and added a reasonable tip.

“Yes,” he said.

After the waiter left, he checked the latch and sat by the window. The toast had softened beneath its cover. He separated the halves of the sandwich so they would not become any wetter.

Across the room, the dead man’s wife approached a bank of microphones.

He muted the television. The news would continue for hours, repeating information already established, adding details that did not concern him.

He had an early checkout.

The prison had no bars. It had a garden, a library, and windows that widened whenever you looked at them, so no inmate could say he had been denied the horizon.

At nine each morning, the windows went dark.

“Rehabilitation session,” said the ceiling.

Elias sat in the white chair and held out his wrists.

He had learned not to make them ask.

***

The first thing he noticed was the cold.

Not the alley. Not the rain. The cold inside her left shoe, where the sole had split and water had worked its way beneath her toes.

He had never known about the shoe.

At trial there had been photographs, diagrams, a chronology reduced to eleven minutes. Her name was Mara Venn. She was thirty-four. She repaired domestic air filters and had a daughter.

In the photograph shown to the jury, she had worn sandals.

Now he was inside the shoe.

He was also inside the small, stubborn worry about getting sick before the end of the month. Inside the ache behind her eyes. Inside the memory of a grocery list she had forgotten to save.

Bread. Pears. Something for breakfast.

Her mind did not know it was approaching the event that would define her to strangers. It was still occupied with an ordinary Thursday.

Then came the footsteps.

Elias knew those footsteps. He had made them.

But knowing did nothing to prepare him for hearing them from ahead.

Mara slowed.

Behind her, he slowed.

A little calculation began—so swift and familiar it seemed older than language. Distance to the avenue. Light in the laundromat. Could she turn without appearing to turn because she was afraid?

He felt her trying not to be insulting.

That was the first thing that broke him.

Even then, with danger gathering behind her, some part of her was concerned with not making a stranger feel accused.

She crossed the street.

The footsteps crossed.

Her thoughts narrowed. The pears vanished. The workday vanished. The world became doors and distances.

The laundromat was closed.

The avenue was farther than she had thought.

There was a man coming toward her.

There was Elias.

***

Afterward, the chair released him.

He bent over and vomited into the basin that rose discreetly from the floor.

“How would you characterize the victim’s emotional state?” asked the ceiling.

He wiped his mouth.

“Afraid.”

“Please be specific.”

He looked toward the black windows.

“Afraid I’d get angry if she ran.”

A pause.

“Progress recorded.”

***

On the seventeenth session, he discovered that terror could contain hope.

He had remembered the night as a sequence of his own decisions: choosing the alley, demanding the bag, pulling her back when she tried to pass. From Mara’s side, nothing was settled.

She could give him the money.

She could tell him the access code.

She could speak gently.

She could mention her daughter.

Each possibility appeared with the force of a solution. Each time, she believed she had found the thing that would let her go home.

He felt the effort it took to keep her voice steady. He felt her watching his face for signs that she had said the right words.

He also heard what he had answered.

In prison he had spent years explaining those words—to his lawyer, to the tribunal, eventually to himself. Here, with Mara’s frightened attention fixed on him, the explanations could not be heard.

***

By the forty-third session, he began dreading the orange.

It rolled out of her bag when it struck the pavement.

One orange, traveling through a thin stream of rainwater.

Mara looked at it.

For a fraction of a second, she thought: That’s going to be bruised.

Then she understood what was happening.

Elias had expected the last moments to become a blur. They did not. Mara noticed things with a clarity that left him nowhere to hide: a loose thread on his cuff, rain trembling on the end of his nose, a lit window above them.

She tried to call toward the window. Her breath failed her, and she tried again.

The crushing weight was in that effort. She still had something to do. There was still someone who might hear. Even as her strength left her, her mind kept issuing instructions to a body that could no longer carry them out.

Breathe.

Lift your hand.

Make a sound.

Then she thought of her daughter waiting at the kitchen table. Not a farewell, not a memory arranged for comfort. She was worried that the child would be alone.

Someone has to tell her.

The thought returned with increasing urgency.

Someone has to tell her.

Elias tried to answer. He tried to promise that someone would. But he had no voice there except the one she had heard that night.

The session ended while she was still afraid.

***

“Your empathy index has stabilized,” the clinician told him.

She sat across from him in the garden. Above them, artificial swallows followed migration patterns no living bird remembered.

“Does that mean I’m rehabilitated?”

“It means we can begin evaluating you.”

He watched a swallow turn.

“Do you have all of it?”

“All of what?”

“Her life. Before.”

“The recovered memory set contains substantial autobiographical material.”

“Could I see some?”

The clinician folded her hands. “Positive memories can reduce the corrective impact.”

“I don’t mean instead.”

She waited.

“I know how she died,” he said. “You make sure I know. But I don’t know what she was like when she wasn’t frightened of me.”

“That isn’t part of your sentence.”

***

The next morning, he sat in the white chair.

The windows darkened.

Cold entered his left shoe.

For an instant there was only the grocery list, the headache, the desire to get home. He paid attention to those things now. He could not save her, and paying attention did not forgive him. Still, he tried to learn what the prison kept hurrying him past.

Mara was choosing between pears and peaches.

Her daughter liked peaches better, but they were expensive this early in the season.

She decided to buy two.

Then, behind her, he heard his footsteps.

He felt her trying not to be insulting.

That was the first thing that broke him.

Even then, with danger gathering behind her, some part of her was concerned with not making a stranger feel accused.

She crossed the street.

The footsteps crossed.

Her thoughts narrowed. The pears vanished. The workday vanished. The world became doors and distances.

The laundromat was closed.

The avenue was farther than she had thought.

There was a man coming toward her.

There was Elias.

Afterward, the chair released him.

He bent over and vomited into the basin that rose discreetly from the floor.

“How would you characterize the victim’s emotional state?” asked the ceiling.

He wiped his mouth.

“Afraid.”

“Please be specific.”

He looked toward the black windows.

“Afraid I’d get angry if she ran.”

A pause.

“Progress recorded.”

On the seventeenth session, he discovered that terror could contain hope.

He had remembered the night as a sequence of his own decisions: choosing the alley, demanding the bag, pulling her back when she tried to pass. From Mara’s side, nothing was settled.

She could give him the money.

She could tell him the access code.

She could speak gently.

She could mention her daughter.

Each possibility appeared with the force of a solution. Each time, she believed she had found the thing that would let her go home.

He felt the effort it took to keep her voice steady. He felt her watching his face for signs that she had said the right words.

He also heard what he had answered.

In prison he had spent years explaining those words—to his lawyer, to the tribunal, eventually to himself. Here, with Mara’s frightened attention fixed on him, the explanations could not be heard.

By the forty-third session, he began dreading the orange.

It rolled out of her bag when it struck the pavement.

One orange, traveling through a thin stream of rainwater.

Mara looked at it.

For a fraction of a second, she thought: That’s going to be bruised.

Then she understood what was happening.

Elias had expected the last moments to become a blur. They did not. Mara noticed things with a clarity that left him nowhere to hide: a loose thread on his cuff, rain trembling on the end of his nose, a lit window above them.

She tried to call toward the window. Her breath failed her, and she tried again.

The crushing weight was in that effort. She still had something to do. There was still someone who might hear. Even as her strength left her, her mind kept issuing instructions to a body that could no longer carry them out.

Breathe.

Lift your hand.

Make a sound.

Then she thought of her daughter waiting at the kitchen table. Not a farewell, not a memory arranged for comfort. She was worried that the child would be alone.

Someone has to tell her.

The thought returned with increasing urgency.

Someone has to tell her.

Elias tried to answer. He tried to promise that someone would. But he had no voice there except the one she had heard that night.

The session ended while she was still afraid.

“Your empathy index has stabilized,” the clinician told him.

She sat across from him in the garden. Above them, artificial swallows followed migration patterns no living bird remembered.

“Does that mean I’m rehabilitated?”

“It means we can begin evaluating you.”

He watched a swallow turn.

“Do you have all of it?”

“All of what?”

“Her life. Before.”

“The recovered memory set contains substantial autobiographical material.”

“Could I see some?”

The clinician folded her hands. “Positive memories can reduce the corrective impact.”

“I don’t mean instead.”

She waited.

“I know how she died,” he said. “You make sure I know. But I don’t know what she was like when she wasn’t frightened of me.”

The next morning, he sat in the white chair.

The windows darkened.

Cold entered his left shoe.

For an instant there was only the grocery list, the headache, the desire to get home. He paid attention to those things now. He could not save her, and paying attention did not forgive him. Still, he tried to learn what the prison kept hurrying him past.

Mara was choosing between pears and peaches.

Her daughter liked peaches better, but they were expensive this early in the season.

She decided to buy two.

Then, behind her, he heard his footsteps.

The mattress dipped.

A spring gave a short, rusty creak just above her ear. She drew her elbow closer to her body, slowly, keeping her sleeve from brushing the hanging sheet.

He settled his weight on the bed.

She still hadn’t taken another breath.

“Your left eye,” the man said, “or your daughter pays for your refusal.”

Mara waited for him to add something. A time limit, perhaps. Some further condition that would make this a problem she could solve rather than a fact she had to survive.

Across the room, her daughter sat with her shoes dangling above the floor. One lace had come undone. Mara kept looking at it. She had meant to teach her the double knot this morning, but they had been late, and she had said, *Tomorrow.*

The knife lay within reach.

She tried to picture herself afterward and couldn’t. Every imagined future stopped at the edge of the table. There was only the room, the blade, her daughter watching her with the terrible confidence that adults knew what to do.

“Please,” Mara said.

The man glanced toward the child.

“No.” The word escaped so quickly it hurt her throat. “No. I understand.”

She reached.

Her arm felt strangely distant until her fingers touched the handle. Then sensation crowded in: the cold metal at its end, a shallow groove beneath her thumb, sweat cooling between her palm and the wood. Her wrist trembled. She pressed her other hand against it, ashamed of the delay, furious that she could still be ashamed of anything.

She did not want to lose her eye. The thought was small and plain and impossible to silence. She wanted to see her daughter grow with both eyes. She wanted to go home without having to become brave.

“Mum?”

Mara looked up. Her daughter’s mouth had begun to shake.

“I’m here,” she said.

She closed her fingers around the handle. It shifted against the tabletop with a faint scrape, an ordinary sound that made her stomach contract.

For one more breath, she left it there.

“You missed a spot.”

“Tell me that again, Lou, and they’ll need a third guy in here.”

Rain ticked against the boarded window. Somewhere upstairs, a television audience applauded.

Lou shifted on his knees. “I’m making conversation.”

“You’re supervising. Conversation is when both people enjoy it.”

“All right. Worst job.”

“This one, if you keep talking.”

“No, career worst.”

Frank sat back on his heels. His knees made two distinct popping sounds.

“Fish market,” he said.

“The one on Delancey?”

“August. Power had been off since Friday. We got there Tuesday.”

Lou stopped scrubbing. “Yeah. Okay.”

“Everybody warned us about the body. Nobody mentioned the squid.”

“I remember your shoes.”

“My wife made me leave them outside.”

“Reasonable.”

“Somebody stole them.”

“That’s this city. There’s always somebody having a worse week.”

Frank leaned forward again. The patch of floor between them had begun to show its original yellow.

Lou said, “Mine was the dentist.”

Frank looked up. “You’ve done twenty-three years of this, and your worst job was a dentist?”

“Back office. Private card game. I don’t like dentists.”

“You weren’t there for an appointment.”

“He had those educational posters. Giant gums. Everywhere I looked, gums.”

“There were three dead men in that room.”

“I know. None of them were showing me what happens if I don’t floss.”

Frank shook his head.

“And the little sink,” Lou continued. “That was what got me. I kept thinking about how many people had spat in it.”

“You are a very particular man.”

“I have standards.”

“You ate a sandwich in the elevator coming up here.”

“It was wrapped.”

The upstairs audience laughed. Frank glanced at the ceiling.

“Someone lives up there?”

“Apparently.”

“They hear anything?”

Lou shrugged. “Nobody’s come down.”

For a while there was only the scrape of their brushes and the rain.

“What about the birthday party?” Frank asked.

Lou closed his eyes. “Don’t.”

“Forty-seven shrimp platters.”

“Forty-eight.”

“You counted?”

“I carried them.”

“The chocolate fountain was still going.”

“Don’t remind me.”

“Little pump working its heart out. Everybody gone, music off, and this thing’s bubbling away.”

“There was a fly in it.”

“There were several flies in it.”

“I was trying to remember it nicer.”

Frank gave a short laugh, then rubbed his nose against his shoulder.

“That wasn’t my worst,” Lou said. “But I didn’t eat chocolate for a year.”

“You ate my Easter egg.”

“White chocolate. Completely different animal.”

A drop of water landed in a bucket by the window.

Frank said, “Remember the apartment with the little dog?”

Lou kept his eyes on the floor. “Yeah.”

“Kept bringing us that ball.”

“Yeah.”

“Put it right down beside my hand.”

“I remember, Frank.”

Frank worked quietly for a moment.

“My daughter’s got a dog now. Same kind, I think.”

“Good dogs.”

“Annoying bark.”

“They’re small. They’ve got to get it out somehow.”

Lou reached for a clean rag, then paused.

“The dog job wasn’t disgusting.”

“No.”

“So it doesn’t count.”

“All right.”

Upstairs, the television went silent. They heard footsteps, a cupboard closing, water running through a pipe in the wall.

Lou inspected the floor.

“You missed a—”

Frank raised his brush.

“—payment,” Lou finished. “On your van. You were telling me.”

Frank held his gaze, then lowered the brush.

“Smart man.”

“Twenty-three years,” Lou said. “You learn when to change the subject.”

The crowd changed direction before Mara understood why.

One moment she was walking; the next, her feet were moving to keep up with the pressure at her back. A shoulder drove beneath her chin. Her arms became trapped against her sides. She tried to turn toward the wall, but there was no room even to twist.

“Wait,” she said.

Nobody could have heard it.

The pressure tightened. She breathed out, and the space she had made was immediately taken. When she tried to inhale, her chest barely moved.

For several seconds she stayed upright without touching the ground.

Then someone fell ahead of her.

Mara pitched forward with three people against her back. Her knees struck pavement. She got one hand down before the weight flattened her, cheek scraping concrete. Somewhere beside her, a woman kept saying a name.

Mara tried to pull her knees beneath her. A shoe landed between her shoulders and slid away. Another came down on her side.

She felt a rib give—a small, distinct crack, followed by pain that stopped her thoughts.

Her mouth opened. No shout came, only a thin breath she could not afford to lose.

Above her, people were pleading with people farther away to stop pushing. They sounded frightened, almost apologetic. Still the weight increased.

She pressed her palm into the pavement. She needed enough room to lift her chest, no more than that. An inch.

A hand caught her wrist.

For a moment it only held her. Then it pulled, hard, and her shoulder moved into a gap. She dragged in a shallow breath that hurt worse than anything she had ever felt.

Before she could take another, the gap began to close.

The lock gave on the third blow.

Mara had thought there would be more time between knowing and doing. Time to remember a face. Time to decide whether the instructions she had carried for eleven years still belonged to her.

Instead there was only the door shuddering in its frame and the pill, chalk-pale against her palm.

She swallowed.

For a moment, nothing changed.

The radiator clicked. Rain dragged crooked lines down the window. In the room next door, a television audience laughed.

Then nausea rose through her, sudden and deep. She put a hand against the desk. Her pulse beat hard in her throat, and when she drew a breath, it seemed to accomplish nothing. She tried again, opening her mouth wider.

The next blow split the wood around the latch.

She had been told it would be quick. She had mistaken that for easy.

Heat climbed into her face. Sweat cooled beneath her collar. The room began to tilt, slowly enough that she tried to correct for it, shifting her weight as though she were standing on a ship. Her knee struck the floor.

She could still hear everything: a man giving an order outside, the scrape of something forced into the broken lock, her own breath turning ragged.

The packet of names was ash in the basin. The transmitter was smashed. There was nothing left for her to do.

Her hand reached for the desk anyway.

That frightened her more than the pain. Somewhere beneath the training, beneath the decision she had already made, her body was still trying to get up.

The door burst inward.

She saw shoes first. Wet leather, grit on the soles. Someone crouched beside her and said something sharply, then repeated it. She could no longer separate the words.

Until then, death had remained an event ahead of her.

Now she understood there would be no afterward in which she could judge whether this had been necessary. No quiet room where she would recover and explain. She had swallowed something, and she could not take it back.

She wanted to tell the man beside her that she had changed her mind.

Her fingers caught his sleeve.

The footsteps stopped whenever Mara stopped.

At first she blamed the echo. The alley was narrow, brick walls leaning over a ribbon of wet pavement, and sounds behaved strangely here. Her heels clicked twice. Somewhere behind her, another pair answered.

She stopped beneath a fire escape.

Silence.

“Very funny,” she said.

Rain ticked against the metal overhead.

At the mouth of the alley stood a man in a pale coat. He was far enough away that she couldn’t see his face, but she could see that he wasn’t sheltering from the rain.

Mara started walking again.

So did he.

She took out her phone. The screen lit her fingers: no service. She tried calling anyway, keeping the phone to her ear while she looked for an open doorway.

Behind her, the footsteps quickened.

She turned.

The man had stopped beneath a streetlamp. One hand pressed against the bricks, the fingers spread. His head hung so low that his chin touched his chest.

“Are you all right?” she asked.

His shoulders jerked.

The sound was small and distinct: a crack like a knuckle being bent too far.

Mara took a step backward.

Another crack followed. Then several together.

The man’s coat shifted across his back. Something beneath it rose, slowly at first, drawing the fabric tight between his shoulders. He braced both hands against the wall. His elbows folded at angles that made Mara instinctively clutch her own arms.

“Oh, God.”

He looked up.

She recognized him then. The man from the nearly empty train carriage. He had watched her in the window’s reflection all the way from Bell Street.

His mouth opened, but the sound came from deep in his chest—a strained, wavering breath that grew rougher as she listened.

His face began to lengthen.

Mara couldn’t make herself look away. His jaw pushed forward beneath skin stretched shiny by the rain. His lips drew back. Teeth that had been ordinary a moment ago crowded his mouth, forcing it wider.

He reached toward her.

His hand struck the streetlamp instead. The fingers spread around the pole, joints swelling and shifting beneath the skin. His nails scraped the metal, leaving pale lines.

Mara ran.

Her heel slipped on the wet pavement. She caught the wall and kept going, scraping her palm along the bricks.

Behind her came the tearing of cloth.

She glanced back once.

The pale coat lay twisted around his waist. Dark hair was spreading across his shoulders and climbing his neck. He crouched in the streetlamp’s light, one leg stretched awkwardly behind him. As she watched, his ankle lifted and his foot lengthened against the ground.

A final series of cracks carried down the alley.

Then he stood.

His head was above the lamp.

Mara hit the service door at the alley’s end with both hands. Locked. She grabbed the handle and shook it.

“Help!”

A heavy footfall sounded behind her.

She struck the door again. Somewhere inside, a television went quiet.

“Please!”

A light appeared beneath the door.

The footsteps stopped.

Mara held the handle with both hands. She could hear someone approaching on the other side, could hear the slow drag of slippers.

Behind her, close enough to stir the hair against her neck, the creature breathed.

The lock began to turn.

By the time they reached the pumping station, Jonah could no longer close his hand.

He kept trying anyway. His fingers curled halfway toward his palm, then opened, as though he were letting something small escape.

“Could be the cold,” Mara said.

Nobody answered her.

Rain tapped the broken skylight. Beyond the walls, something dragged itself along the fence, stopped, and dragged itself farther. The dead had patience. It was one of the things Eli hated most about them.

Jonah sat against a pump housing with his bitten arm tucked under his coat.

“Let me see,” Tess said.

“You saw.”

“I want to see again.”

He let her pull the sleeve back. She examined the wound, then pressed two fingers against his wrist. Eli watched her face. She had been a veterinarian before, which was close enough now that everyone expected her to know what to do.

“Well?” Mara asked.

Tess lowered Jonah’s sleeve.

Mara looked away first.

They had seen it happen twice. Fever, confusion, a brief quiet that seemed like recovery. Then the person stopped breathing. Then, sometimes before anyone had begun to cry, they moved again.

“We can wait,” Mara said. “There’s a storeroom. We put him in there, we lock the door—”

“No,” Jonah said.

“You don’t get to say no to every idea.”

“I get to say no to that one.”

Mara crouched beside him. She was his younger sister, though in the last six months she had begun speaking to him like an exhausted parent.

“Then we tie you. Just until morning.”

Jonah looked toward the storeroom. Its door was dented inward near the handle. Somebody had once tried very hard to get out.

He shook his head.

Eli felt the weight of the pistol beneath his jacket. He had carried it for so long that he usually forgot it was there. Now the others kept glancing at him.

Tess stood. “We should all agree.”

“No,” Mara said. “Don’t make this something we vote on.”

“I didn’t mean—”

“What did you mean?”

Tess had no answer. She went to the skylight and stood beneath its leaking edge, letting rain darken one shoulder.

Jonah fumbled at the fastening of his coat. Mara helped him.

“Inside pocket,” he told her.

She took out a folded envelope.

“Those are the seeds,” she said.

“I know.”

“You’re giving me seeds?”

“Keep them dry.”

She stared at him, then pushed the envelope back into his pocket.

“You can carry them.”

For a while, all they heard was the rain.

Then Jonah began to shiver. His heels knocked against the concrete, and he looked down at them with frightened irritation, as if they belonged to someone embarrassing him in public.

Eli knelt.

“Jonah.”

“Not yet.”

“All right.”

Jonah swallowed. “I’m trying to think of something.”

Nobody asked what.

His gaze moved from Tess to Mara, then settled on Eli.

“There was a place,” he said. “Before. We went there after your wedding.”

“The diner?”

“Yeah. What was it called?”

Eli couldn’t remember.

Jonah waited.

“The one with the blue tables,” Eli said.

“I know which one.”

“Denny’s?” Tess offered.

“No.”

Mara laughed once, sharply, and covered her mouth.

Jonah smiled at her. For a moment his face was familiar enough that Eli nearly believed they could stay like this: tired people sheltering from bad weather, trying to remember the name of a restaurant.

Then Jonah’s smile slackened.

He turned to Mara. “You should go outside.”

“No.”

“Please.”

“No. You don’t get that either.”

He nodded, accepting it.

Eli took out the pistol and held it low beside his leg.

Tess turned from the window. “Are you certain?”

Jonah looked at her, but Eli wasn’t sure whom she had asked.

“No,” Eli said.

His voice sounded too loud in the room.

“I’m not certain about anything.”

Jonah reached for him with his good hand. Eli took it.

“I am,” Jonah whispered. Then, after a pause: “I’m scared, though.”

Mara leaned against her brother, pressing her forehead to his temple.

“I know.”

“I don’t want—”

“I know.”

He shut his eyes. His hand tightened around Eli’s, then loosened enough to let him move away.

The shot filled the pumping station.

Afterward, Mara kept her forehead against Jonah’s for several seconds. Then she drew back and looked at him.

Eli waited for her to say something. To accuse him, thank him, ask him to leave.

She buttoned Jonah’s coat.

Her hands were clumsy. She put one button through the wrong hole and had to start again.

Tess sat down on the floor.

Outside, the thing at the fence resumed its slow progress.

They stayed until the light began to fade. At last Mara reached into Jonah’s pocket and took the envelope. One corner had softened with sweat. She held it carefully by the edges.

“The Orchard,” she said.

Eli looked at her.

“The diner. It was called the Orchard.”

He remembered then: the chipped blue tables, Jonah stealing fries from his plate, all of them lingering because nobody had anywhere urgent to be.

“Yes,” he said.

But Jonah was the one who had wanted to know.

By the time they reached the pumping station, Jonah could no longer close his hand.

He kept trying anyway. His fingers curled halfway toward his palm, then opened, as though he were letting something small escape.

“Could be the cold,” Mara said.

Nobody answered her.

Rain tapped the broken skylight. Beyond the walls, something dragged itself along the fence, stopped, and dragged itself farther. The dead had patience. It was one of the things Eli hated most about them.

Jonah sat against a pump housing with his bitten arm tucked under his coat.

“Let me see,” Tess said.

“You saw.”

“I want to see again.”

He let her pull the sleeve back. She examined the wound, then pressed two fingers against his wrist. Eli watched her face. She had been a veterinarian before, which was close enough now that everyone expected her to know what to do.

“Well?” Mara asked.

Tess lowered Jonah’s sleeve.

Mara looked away first.

They had seen it happen twice. Fever, confusion, a brief quiet that seemed like recovery. Then the person stopped breathing. Then, sometimes before anyone had begun to cry, they moved again.

“We can wait,” Mara said. “There’s a storeroom. We put him in there, we lock the door—”

“No,” Jonah said.

“You don’t get to say no to every idea.”

“I get to say no to that one.”

Mara crouched beside him. She was his younger sister, though in the last six months she had begun speaking to him like an exhausted parent.

“Then we tie you. Just until morning.”

Jonah looked toward the storeroom. Its door was dented inward near the handle. Somebody had once tried very hard to get out.

He shook his head.

Eli felt the weight of the pistol beneath his jacket. He had carried it for so long that he usually forgot it was there. Now the others kept glancing at him.

Tess stood. “We should all agree.”

“No,” Mara said. “Don’t make this something we vote on.”

“I didn’t mean—”

“What did you mean?”

Tess had no answer. She went to the skylight and stood beneath its leaking edge, letting rain darken one shoulder.

Jonah fumbled at the fastening of his coat. Mara helped him.

“Inside pocket,” he told her.

She took out a folded envelope.

“Those are the seeds,” she said.

“I know.”

“You’re giving me seeds?”

“Keep them dry.”

She stared at him, then pushed the envelope back into his pocket.

“You can carry them.”

For a while, all they heard was the rain.

Then Jonah began to shiver. His heels knocked against the concrete, and he looked down at them with frightened irritation, as if they belonged to someone embarrassing him in public.

Eli knelt.

“Jonah.”

“Not yet.”

“All right.”

Jonah swallowed. “I’m trying to think of something.”

Nobody asked what.

His gaze moved from Tess to Mara, then settled on Eli.

“There was a place,” he said. “Before. We went there after your wedding.”

“The diner?”

“Yeah. What was it called?”

Eli couldn’t remember.

Jonah waited.

“The one with the blue tables,” Eli said.

“I know which one.”

“Denny’s?” Tess offered.

“No.”

Mara laughed once, sharply, and covered her mouth.

Jonah smiled at her. For a moment his face was familiar enough that Eli nearly believed they could stay like this: tired people sheltering from bad weather, trying to remember the name of a restaurant.

Then Jonah’s smile slackened.

He turned to Mara. “You should go outside.”

“No.”

“Please.”

“No. You don’t get that either.”

He nodded, accepting it.

Eli took out the pistol and held it low beside his leg.

Tess turned from the window. “Are you certain?”

Jonah looked at her, but Eli wasn’t sure whom she had asked.

“No,” Eli said.

His voice sounded too loud in the room.

“I’m not certain about anything.”

Jonah reached for him with his good hand. Eli took it.

“I am,” Jonah whispered. Then, after a pause: “I’m scared, though.”

Mara leaned against her brother, pressing her forehead to his temple.

“I know.”

“I don’t want—”

“I know.”

He shut his eyes. His hand tightened around Eli’s, then loosened enough to let him move away.

The shot filled the pumping station.

Afterward, Mara kept her forehead against Jonah’s for several seconds. Then she drew back and looked at him.

Eli waited for her to say something. To accuse him, thank him, ask him to leave.

She buttoned Jonah’s coat.

Her hands were clumsy. She put one button through the wrong hole and had to start again.

Tess sat down on the floor.

Outside, the thing at the fence resumed its slow progress.

They stayed until the light began to fade. At last Mara reached into Jonah’s pocket and took the envelope. One corner had softened with sweat. She held it carefully by the edges.

“The Orchard,” she said.

Eli looked at her.

“The diner. It was called the Orchard.”

He remembered then: the chipped blue tables, Jonah stealing fries from his plate, all of them lingering because nobody had anywhere urgent to be.

“Yes,” he said.

But Jonah was the one who had wanted to know.

results.model_response:
For the first week, he slept better than he had in years.

This would trouble him later.

He had expected punishment to announce itself: sirens, a fist against the door, his own conscience speaking in a voice he could not ignore. Instead there were ordinary mornings. Bread browned in the toaster. Rain collected in the gutter. Once, standing in line for coffee, he laughed at something the woman ahead of him said.

He had killed a man, and still he knew when something was funny.

The first sighting came on a Tuesday.

A dark shape stood at the edge of the kitchen doorway. He turned, already preparing some harmless remark, and found his coat hanging from a hook.

He moved the coat into the cupboard.

Two days later the shape was beside the window.

That time, nothing was there to explain it.

Afterward he began turning his head quickly. In the street, at his desk, while brushing his teeth. His neck ached by evening. People occasionally glanced behind themselves when speaking to him, trying to discover what had caught his attention.

“Nothing,” he said.

He became very good at saying it.

***

At first, the ghost was only a mistake his eyes made: a shoulder where shadows overlapped, a pale oval in a darkened pane. It vanished whenever he looked directly at it.

So he stopped looking directly.

He watched the corner of the room while pretending to read. He held a spoon suspended over his breakfast until milk dripped onto his trousers. When the figure appeared, he tried to remain perfectly still, as if stillness might persuade it to stay.

He wanted proof that it was there.

Then, when it lingered, he wanted anything else.

***

Memory began to spoil.

He could remember the murder well enough, though never in the order he wanted. He tried to summon the argument, the provocation, the moment that would make everything afterward seem inevitable. Instead he remembered the victim crouching to tie a shoelace before entering the room.

Or the little sound he had made when surprised.

Once he remembered him laughing, and could not place the occasion. He spent half a day trying. By evening the laughter seemed to belong to every conversation they had ever had.

His reasons, once so solid, grew difficult to recite. He wrote them down. Reading them the following morning, he was embarrassed by their smallness and furious at the dead man for having made them small.

That night the figure appeared beside his bed.

It did not accuse him. It seemed to be waiting for him to finish.

***

He began sleeping with the lights on.

Then he discovered that lights made corners.

He bought brighter bulbs. He removed a bookcase. He dragged the wardrobe away from the wall and left it standing in the middle of the bedroom, where he bruised his hip against it each morning. Eventually he slept on the kitchen floor because he could see both doorways from there.

He still went to work.

There were reports to submit and passwords to reset. He found this increasingly offensive. A colleague asked whether he had enjoyed the weekend, and he stared at her until she apologized.

He did not know what she was apologizing for.

Neither, apparently, did she.

***

By the third month, the ghost had acquired habits.

It stood nearer when he lied. It appeared in reflections when someone spoke kindly to him. It waited beside strangers who had the victim’s height, or hands, or way of lifting their chin.

He understood, sometimes, that he was inventing these rules.

Understanding did not help him disobey them.

He stopped using mirrors. He answered questions with painful precision. Asked whether he was all right, he said, “I got here safely.”

Asked if he needed anything, he began to cry.

***

The worst part was not fear.

It was how much of his life he surrendered without noticing.

He stopped listening to music because he needed to hear the apartment. He stopped cooking because standing with his back to the room was unbearable. He stopped calling his sister after she said, gently, that he sounded far away.

There were days when he spoke only to the shape.

At first he pleaded. Later he explained. Finally, exhausted by his own arguments, he described whatever he was doing.

“I’m putting the kettle on.”

“I can’t find the other sock.”

“It’s raining again.”

The figure never answered.

One evening he realized he had begun leaving space for it when he passed through a doorway.

He stood there for a long time, pressed against the frame, waiting for the dead man to go first.

The room had no windows, but he kept looking for the sky.

It was a foolish thing to want. He knew where he was: underground, a prisoner, with a guard beside the door. Before they covered his face, he had seen a crack in the ceiling and a pale root pushing through it.

He tried to remember that root now.

“Where did your unit cross?”

He had answered already. He had given them the name of the town, the road, everything he actually knew. They kept asking for a bridge.

Then the water came, and there was no room left in him for the question.

His body believed he was drowning. The knowledge that he was on dry land remained somewhere in his mind, precise and useless. There was a floor beneath him. A ceiling above. Someone nearby could breathe without thinking about it.

He tried to reach that ordinary fact.

Panic took it away.

He pulled against what held him. He knew he was doing it, knew it would not help, and could not stop. He wanted to turn his face. He wanted a moment in which nobody touched him. His thoughts dwindled until they were no longer words, only the demand that this end.

When it stopped, he heard himself making a sound he did not recognize.

“Which bridge?”

He stared toward the voice. For a moment he could not remember what a bridge was.

The guard shifted. Water moved in a container.

“No,” he said at once.

The interrogator waited.

He searched his memory desperately: roads, villages, a railway embankment glimpsed from a truck. He could give them a name. Any name might buy him another minute. But they would ask what it looked like, who had guarded it, where they had gone afterward.

“Please,” he said. “I’m trying to remember.”

And he was—though now, more than anything, he was trying to remember the ceiling, and the root, and how the room had looked before he knew what could happen in it.

The bounty on Iven Marr was worth six months of oxygen.

That was how Vale measured money now—not in credits, but in how long she could keep her ship breathing.

She found him beneath the artificial dawn of Ceres Station, slipping through a market where vendors sold printed fruit and memories of rain. Her visor marked him in amber.

**IVEN MARR. ALIVE.**

“Marr,” she called.

He looked back once, then tipped a cart of glass peaches into her path.

Vale vaulted it. Marr ran between stalls, shoulder-checking a service drone, and reached a maintenance hatch before she caught his coat.

He twisted out of it. A ceramic knife appeared in his hand.

“Walk away.”

“Can’t afford to.”

He slashed at her face. The blade scored her visor, filling one corner of her vision with static. She caught his wrist, but he drove a knee into her ribs and tore free.

Vale staggered against the hatch. Her next breath came shallow.

Marr glanced toward the crowd. A child stood frozen beside the overturned cart.

Vale drew her pulse caster.

“Drop it.”

He lunged.

The weapon cracked sharply. Two tethered contacts struck his jacket and bit through the fabric. For a fraction of a second, he kept coming.

Then the current caught him.

His body went rigid—not lifted or thrown, but abruptly robbed of coordination. The pulses overwhelmed the ordinary signals passing between nerves and muscles. His shoulders drew tight, his legs stiffened, and the knife fell from fingers he could no longer command.

A strangled sound escaped him. His jaw clenched. The muscles across his chest and abdomen contracted hard enough to interrupt the breath he had been taking.

Vale released the trigger as he toppled.

She caught one shoulder, turning his fall away from the edge of the hatch, but his knees still struck the deck with a heavy crack. He landed on his side and curled around himself.

The market had gone quiet.

Marr dragged in a ragged breath, then another. His hands trembled. The forced contractions had left his muscles aching, and sharp pain lingered where the contacts had struck. He tried to push himself upright; his elbow buckled.

“Stay down,” Vale said, holstering the caster.

He stared at her with unfocused anger. “You said alive.”

“That’s still the plan.”

She knelt beyond kicking distance and swept her scanner over him. Breathing rapid. Pulse racing. No obvious rhythm abnormality on the portable readout, though that was no guarantee.

The manufacturers liked the phrase *nonlethal*. Vale had seen enough station reports to distrust it. Electrical weapons could disrupt heart rhythms; falls could break skulls. High voltage was not a promise that someone would get back up.

She called for medical support.

While they waited, she moved the knife out of reach and secured Marr’s wrists in front of him. He flinched when the restraint brushed one of the contacts.

“Don’t pull those,” she said. “Let the medic do it.”

He looked past her at the spilled peaches. A vendor was gathering the unbroken ones into a crate.

“How much?” Marr asked.

Vale checked that he was still breathing easily.

“For you?”

He nodded.

“Six months.”

He frowned, not understanding.

She didn’t explain. Above them, the station’s artificial dawn brightened toward morning, and somewhere beyond its hull her empty ship waited for air.

The first thing Mara tried was being polite.

“Hello?”

Her voice came back from the tiled walls smaller than it had left her.

She sat in a bolted chair with her right forearm inside a steel housing. A yellow button rested beneath her free hand. Beyond the chair stood a door with a green EXIT sign above it, absurdly cheerful.

A speaker clicked.

The recorded voice explained the arrangement once. Press the button, endure what the mechanism did to her trapped hand, and the door would open.

Mara waited for the rest: the riddle, the loophole, the admission that this was a test of whether she would refuse.

Instead, a clock lit up.

**04:00.**

“No,” she said.

She pulled at her arm. The housing struck the bolts beneath the chair with a solid clunk. She tried standing, twisting, bracing both feet against the floor. Nothing shifted except the chair cushion. She shouted until she had to stop and swallow.

**03:26.**

She inspected everything she could reach. The button’s rim. The screws beneath the seat. A short length of cable disappearing into the wall. One screw turned a fraction under her thumbnail, and hope arrived so suddenly that she laughed.

Then her nail slipped. The screw would go no farther.

She sat still, holding her free hand against her chest.

She knew that hand. She knew the trapped one, too: the small white scar beside its thumb, the finger that stiffened in winter. That morning she had used it to hold a mug while searching for her keys. She remembered setting the mug down carefully so it wouldn’t leave a ring.

She tried not to imagine explaining its absence.

**02:41.**

Perhaps someone was coming. Someone might already have heard her. If she pressed now and rescuers arrived ten seconds later—

She screamed again, listening between each cry.

Only the clock answered.

The yellow button was broad enough for her palm. She placed her hand above it, then snatched it away before touching it.

Her body seemed to have reached a decision without consulting her. Her shoulder drew back. Her stomach tightened. Every time she leaned forward, her free arm locked at the elbow.

“Just put your hand there,” she whispered.

She couldn’t.

For a while she hated herself for that. Then she looked at the steel casing and understood how unreasonable it was to demand calm.

She planted both feet. The left one kept sliding, so she moved it beneath the chair. She loosened her jaw and took a breath that broke halfway in. Another came more easily.

She pressed her back against the cushion. Not readying herself for pain, exactly. Giving herself somewhere to be when it happened.

**01:09.**

She thought of calling out a name. Her sister’s came first, but saying it into this room felt unbearable.

Instead she said, “I want to go home.”

Her palm settled on the button.

She stayed there, shaking, while the seconds changed. She was still searching the walls. Still listening. Some stubborn part of her expected a voice to interrupt and tell her she could stop.

At thirty seconds, she closed her eyes.

Then she opened them again. She wanted to see the door.

results.model_response:
The plank bowed beneath Tomas’s bare feet.

Behind him, the deck of the *Mercy’s End* lay silent. No creak of a boot, no whispered wager. Even the men who had sworn to stand beside him now found reasons to study the rigging.

Captain Vale stood at the rail with Tomas’s stolen pistol tucked into her sash.

“You promised them my ship,” she said.

Tomas glanced back. The cutlass nearest his spine moved forward an inch.

“Captain, I only meant—”

“I heard what you meant through the cabin door.”

Below, the water was so clear he could see the shadow of the hull falling away into blue. Something pale moved at its edge. A shark turned slowly beneath the plank, its gray back slipping through sunlight, its tail sweeping without hurry.

Then Tomas saw another.

His toes curled against the wood.

“Please.”

It came out thinly. He hated that more than he expected. All morning, bound to the mast, he had prepared words about unfair shares and the men lost in Vale’s last raid. Now he could remember none of them.

The ship rolled. He threw out his arms, rope rasping between his bound wrists, and someone on deck drew a sharp breath.

A fin broke the surface below him.

Tomas stared at it. The shark passed beneath his dangling shadow, vanished under the plank, and appeared on the other side. Farther out, a second fin traced a wide curve toward the ship.

“Look at me,” Vale said.

He turned his head.

For a moment he thought she might relent. She had once hauled him out of a burning longboat with her own hands. He remembered her grip on his coat, the furious way she had shouted at him to keep breathing.

Now she held out his pistol.

“Was it loaded?”

He said nothing.

“Tomas.”

“Yes.”

She lowered it.

The sailor behind him advanced. Tomas took another step and felt empty air beneath his heel.

“No,” he whispered.

The plank lifted with the swell. His knees shook so violently that he crouched, trying to steady himself, trying to make his body understand that it must not move.

Below him, a gray shape turned.

He looked back once more, searching the faces along the rail.

“Someone,” he said.

The cutlass touched his shirt.

Tomas stepped away from it.

At first, Mara thought the pressure around her ribs was someone holding her.

Then she looked down.

The straps had twisted beneath her arms, biting through her shirt. A hard rectangular shape rested against her sternum. Wires looped across it, some smooth and rubbery, one with a rough seam that caught the pad of her thumb.

She stopped touching it.

Tick.

The sound was so small she almost mistook it for a fingernail tapping the underside of a table.

Tick.

“No,” she said, quietly, as if correcting a mistake.

She pulled her shoulders back. The straps tightened. Something cold pressed through the thin cotton over her breastbone, and she froze with her breath half taken. She tried to finish inhaling without moving her chest.

Her fingers hovered over the wires. A yellow one trembled. For one bewildered second she thought it was moving by itself. Then she saw that her hand was shaking against it.

“Okay. Okay.”

She searched the room for someone to answer her. A chair. A closed door. Her coat on the floor. Ordinary things, all exactly where they ought to be.

Tick.

She called for help, but her voice came out too softly. She swallowed and tried again.

“Help!”

The shout hurt against the straps. She grabbed at them, then jerked her hands away, terrified of what she might loosen, what she might touch. Her palms stayed open beside her face.

“Please,” she said to the empty room. “Please, somebody.”

Now she could hear the ticking beneath everything: her quick breaths, her shoes scraping the floor, the broken, rising sound coming from her own throat. She backed into the door and fumbled behind her for the handle, sobbing because she could not find it, because it was there, it had to be there, and her fingers would not work.

The power was out in the hall, but the microwave clock still glowed in the kitchen.

Claire stopped with her hand on the light switch.

She pressed it down, then up again. Nothing.

“Great.”

Rain ticked against the window above the sink. She could hear the refrigerator running and, somewhere upstairs, the soft knock of a pipe. Ordinary sounds. She stood listening to them longer than she needed to.

Behind the half-open basement door, a man watched her take off her shoes.

He hadn’t expected that. He’d expected her to go straight upstairs. Now she was bending over in the hall, one hand braced against the wall, close enough that he could hear the wet lace drag through an eyelet.

He held the knife against his thigh to keep it from touching the door.

Claire left her shoes on the mat. One fell sideways with a dull thump, and she flinched.

“Jesus.”

Her phone was in her handbag. She found a receipt, a loose mint, the loop of her keys. Not the phone.

She remembered setting it in the cup holder.

For a moment she considered putting her shoes back on. Instead, she dropped the bag on the little hall table and started toward the kitchen. There were candles in a drawer. Or a flashlight. Ben kept moving the flashlight.

The edge of the runner caught beneath her sock.

She stumbled, struck her shoulder against the wall, and reached out for balance. Her palm landed on the basement door.

It moved inward an inch.

Behind it, the man shifted his weight onto his back foot.

Claire caught herself. Her shoulder hurt. She stood still, waiting for the sharpness to settle, her fingers resting against the painted wood.

The basement smelled damp.

She usually kept that door shut.

She tried to remember coming down that morning with the laundry basket. Had she latched it? She could picture the basket, the blue towel hanging over its side, but not the door.

Her fingers curled around the edge.

Then the refrigerator motor stopped.

The sudden quiet made her lift her head.

There had been another sound beneath it. A scrape, perhaps. Cloth against wood.

“Ben?”

She regretted saying it. Ben was in Manchester. She had spoken to him twenty minutes ago, heard the hotel television in the background.

No answer came.

She let go of the door.

In the kitchen, the microwave clock read 11:43. Its green light reached only as far as the counter. Everything below that was a shape she had to recognize: stool, bin, shopping bag.

She opened the drawer beside the sink slowly, keeping her eyes on the hall.

Cutlery shifted.

Wrong drawer.

She shut it without letting it click and opened the next. Tea towels. Batteries. She pushed her hand beneath them and felt the rubber grip of the flashlight.

The beam came on weak and yellow.

She aimed it at the hall.

Her handbag sat where she’d left it. Her shoes were on the mat. The basement door was open a little wider.

Claire lowered the flashlight.

Perhaps she had pushed it farther when she fell.

She took one step toward the back door, placing her foot carefully. Then another.

The lock had always been stiff. She’d meant to ask the landlord about it. To open it, she had to pull the door toward her while turning the key.

She reached behind herself and found the key already in the lock.

From the hall came a quiet wooden click.

The basement door had touched the wall.

Claire pulled on the back door. Turned the key.

It would not move.

“Come on,” she breathed.

A floorboard creaked.

She pulled harder, hurting her fingers, and the key turned at last.

As she lifted the latch, the flashlight beam swung across the hall.

A shoe. A hand.

The knife caught the light.

Claire dropped the flashlight and threw her whole weight against the door.
