He crouched beneath the firing step with his shoulders jammed against the trench wall, trying to make himself small enough to escape the air. His first breath had stung. Now every breath scraped. The muscles in his neck stood out as he dragged at the mask, certain it was choking him, then clamped it back against his face with both hands.

The coughing bent him double. It came in hard, involuntary bursts that left no space to breathe between them. When he finally managed an inhalation, it was thin and whistling, followed by a wet rattle deep in his chest. His throat felt scalded. Tears streamed into the mask’s seal; through the fogged lenses, the duckboards and the man beside him dissolved into uncertain shapes. He tried to call out, but his voice emerged as a scraped whisper and broke into another fit.

At first he could still think in instructions: *Keep the seal tight. Get out of the low ground. Find the ladder.* Then the lack of air narrowed everything. He could see the ladder a few yards away, but could not work out how to reach it while holding the mask with both hands. His fingers trembled. One knee would not straighten.

Someone caught his sleeve. He struck at the hand before recognizing it as help. Shame came and vanished almost at once; there was no room for it. There was only the next breath, the terrible pause before it, and the certainty that if he stopped concentrating for even a moment, his body would forget how.

Rain tapped the windows behind Bellini’s desk. He let it fill the silence while Marco stood on the other side, hat in hand.

“Sit.”

“I’d rather stand.”

Bellini looked up. “That wasn’t a courtesy.”

Marco sat.

On the desk lay a photograph of a man leaving a federal building. Bellini turned it with two fingers.

“Paulie’s developed an interest in public service.”

“We don’t know what he told them.”

“No,” Bellini said. “And I dislike learning things in court.”

Marco studied the photograph. Paulie was smiling at someone outside the frame.

“He’s been with us twenty years.”

“I know. I paid for eighteen of them.”

Beyond the door, a telephone rang. Someone answered it, and the office went quiet again.

Bellini opened a drawer and took out an envelope.

“His wife gets this every month. Same amount. No interruptions.”

Marco didn’t touch it.

“And Paulie?”

“Paulie’s retiring.”

“Does he know?”

“That’s what I’m asking you to take care of.”

Marco glanced toward the window. “I could put him on a plane. Make sure he understands he can’t come back.”

“He understood that before he went into that building.”

Bellini slid the photograph across the desk.

“I want his chair empty tomorrow. Permanently.”

For a moment, Marco looked as though he might say something else. Instead, he took the photograph and tucked it inside his coat.

“The family will ask.”

“They’ll ask you?”

“Eventually.”

“Then let them.”

Marco rose, leaving the envelope where it was.

Bellini tapped it once. “You forgot something.”

Marco picked it up.

At the door, he paused. “He’ll want to talk to you.”

Bellini reached for the telephone.

“He had that opportunity.”

The first shovelful struck the lid like a knock.

He stopped breathing to listen.

The second came heavier—a loose, rattling spill that rolled across the wood above his face. Then another. The hollow drumming thickened into dull thuds as the earth piled up, swallowing the sound of the shovel, the footsteps, the world.

“No.” He meant to shout it, but the word caught in his throat. He tried again. “No, I’m here.”

He pushed against the lid. There was barely room to straighten his wrists. His elbows struck the sides, and the discovery—that he could not even arrange his body to fight—sent a panic through him so violent he bucked against the boards.

The coffin did not move.

Above him, something creaked.

He froze with both palms pressed flat. The wood carried a faint vibration, then settled against his hands. He pictured the dirt gathering overhead, filling every gap around the box. There was nowhere for the lid to go, even if he could break its fastenings.

He clawed at it anyway.

His fingernails skittered across the smooth underside until one found a seam. He dug there, scraping, pulling, worrying the same narrow place. A splinter came loose. He seized it with sudden, desperate hope, then lost it in the dark beside his shoulder.

He couldn’t turn far enough to find it.

His breathing grew loud and quick. He tried to slow it, but each restrained breath ended in a gulp. The air smelled of unfinished wood and his own sweat.

He screamed once more, then held perfectly still, listening for an answer.

In the silence, a few grains of soil sifted through the seam and landed on his lips.

The cup rattled once against its saucer.

At first, he looked merely offended, as though the tea had disappointed him. He swallowed again and pressed two fingers beneath his waistcoat.

“Rather warm in here,” he said.

Beyond the parlour windows, November rain silvered the glass. She sat beside the hearth with her hands folded, watching a bead of perspiration descend from his temple.

He tugged at his collar. The colour had begun to leave his face, except for two uneven patches high upon his cheeks. When he reached for his handkerchief, his fingers trembled so violently that he dropped it.

Then the pain bent him forward.

His breath escaped in a short, astonished gasp. One hand clamped across his stomach; the other searched blindly for the arm of the chair. He tried to speak, but a spasm of retching interrupted him. Tea spilled across the carpet.

She rose, though she did not approach.

He looked up at her. His lips moved around her name without quite forming it. Sweat shone along his upper lip, and his breathing came rapidly now, each breath shallower than the last.

When he attempted to stand, his knees gave way.

The fall shook the teaspoons in their tray. On the carpet, his limbs jerked briefly, then stiffened. His heel struck the brass fender twice. She watched the muscles at his jaw tighten and release.

Afterwards, there was only the uneven movement of his chest.

She knelt at last, careful to keep her skirts clear of the spilled tea. His eyes shifted towards her, struggling to focus.

Behind them, the kettle began to sing.

The ration board flickered above the arena.

**VICTOR: THIRTY MEALS.**
**DECEASED: DEPENDENTS COMPENSATED AT MUNICIPAL DISCRETION.**

Mara tried not to look at the second line.

Across the sand, the man with the spear was coughing into his elbow. He was older than her, perhaps fifty, with a sanitation worker’s orange stripe tattooed around his wrist. Someone in the stands called his name.

“Eli!”

He glanced up. A mistake, but Mara didn’t move.

The loudspeaker crackled.

“Failure to engage constitutes joint forfeiture.”

Eli looked back at her. His spear trembled.

“How many?” he asked.

She knew what he meant. “Two.”

“One,” he said. “My wife.”

The audience sat behind reinforced glass, arranged by district. No one cheered anymore. They watched with the fixed attention of people waiting to learn whether they would eat.

A warning light came on beneath the ration board.

Eli lowered his spear.

“Sorry,” he said, and charged.

Mara caught the shaft against the short blade they had given her. The impact jolted her wrist. She stumbled, and his second thrust cut through her sleeve. For a moment they were close enough that she could smell the laundry soap on his collar.

He had washed his clothes for this.

She backed away. He followed, breathing hard, keeping the point between them. When he thrust again, the spearhead lodged in the padded seam beneath her arm. She clamped her elbow down before he could pull it free.

Both of them tugged. Then Eli let go.

His hands went toward her knife, too late.

Mara stepped inside his reach and drove the blade into his chest.

His breath stopped with a small, startled sound. He gripped her shoulder, and she braced against his weight, unable to make herself pull away. For a few seconds they stood together.

Then his knees folded.

She lowered him awkwardly onto the sand. His lips moved, but she couldn’t hear him over the announcement.

“Decisive action. Full allotment awarded.”

Mara knelt beside him until an attendant ordered her to stand.

At the exit, a dispenser counted thirty meal vouchers into a metal tray. She took them with her uninjured hand.

“His wife,” she said. “Where does she collect?”

The attendant checked his screen.

“Dependent compensation has been declined.”

Behind Mara, the arena crew dragged a rake across the sand. The attendant held out a receipt for her signature.

Mara’s speedometer shivered past ninety.

A horn blared as she cut between a delivery van and a taxi, close enough to snap her side mirror against the van’s door. The impact cracked like a bone. She flinched but kept her foot down, heart beating so hard she could feel it in her teeth.

In the rearview mirror, the black sedan followed.

She twisted, thrust the pistol toward the broken rear window, and fired. The report filled the car, leaving a shrill ringing in her ears. She didn’t see where the bullet went.

When she faced forward, a woman was stepping off the curb with a stroller.

Mara wrenched the wheel. Tires screamed. The woman dragged the stroller backward and fell hard on one knee as Mara’s bumper swept past. In the mirror, she saw the woman folded over the stroller, gripping both sides of it.

“Stop,” Mara whispered, though she didn’t know whether she meant the sedan, the woman, or herself.

Traffic thickened ahead. Brake lights flared beneath an overpass. A bus drifted into her lane, its windows crowded with faces, and she caught a glimpse of a little boy watching her with his mouth open.

The pistol felt slick in her hand. She dropped it onto the passenger seat and put both hands on the wheel.

Behind her, another shot cracked. A neat white hole appeared low in the windshield.

Mara ducked without meaning to. The car wandered across the lane line; someone leaned on a horn, long and furious. She pulled it straight, fighting the urge to close her eyes.

There was nowhere empty to go. Every gap ahead contained someone trying to get home.

The forest went silent when Mara stopped running.

No insects. No owl calls. Only her breath, dragging painfully through her throat, and somewhere behind her, the soft compression of leaves beneath a careful foot.

She pressed herself against an oak. Bark bit through her shirt. In the dark, every gap between the trees seemed deep enough to conceal a person.

Then came a small, hard click.

She turned toward it.

The bolt passed her ear with a thin, vicious whistle and struck the trunk beside her face.

Mara recoiled. For a moment she couldn’t breathe or move. The shaft quivered inches from her eye. A loose strand of her hair clung to its fletching.

She put a hand to her ear, expecting blood. Her fingers came away clean.

Somewhere beyond the oak, something creaked under tension.

Reloading.

She ran.

Branches lashed her cheeks. Roots caught at her shoes. She held one hand in front of her, unable to see far enough ahead to choose a path. Her own crashing footsteps covered every sound the hunter might make.

At a fallen tree she stumbled, caught herself, and nearly cried out. She stayed crouched there, one palm sunk in wet moss, listening so hard her jaw ached.

Nothing.

She tried to remember which side of her head the bolt had passed. If she knew that, perhaps she could keep the trunk between them. But she had turned when she heard the click, and now she couldn’t remember how far.

A leaf stirred nearby.

Mara clamped both hands over her mouth.

The dog found him behind the gutted pharmacy, with half a strip of dried meat caught between his teeth.

For a moment, neither moved.

Its ribs showed through its filthy coat. One ear was torn. It stared at his mouth, and he understood with a sick clarity that it was as hungry as he was.

He tried to swallow.

The dog lunged.

Its weight knocked him against the brickwork. His head struck hard enough to fill his vision with white sparks, and then its teeth caught his forearm. He shouted and hit it with his free hand, short, clumsy blows that did nothing. The meat fell into the ash.

He saw it lying there.

That was worse than the pain.

Three days of chewing boiled leather. Three days of standing too quickly and finding the world tipping beneath him. That morning he had caught himself studying a dead beetle on a windowsill, trying to remember whether bright colors meant poison.

He drove his knee upward. The dog released him and snapped again, catching his sleeve. Cloth tore. He fell with it, scraping his face along the pavement, one hand reaching blindly through broken glass.

His fingers closed around a brick.

The first blow glanced off. The second made the dog stumble away, yelping. He scrambled onto his knees and raised the brick again, shouting until his dry throat failed him.

The dog stayed just beyond his reach. It trembled, favoring one leg, but its eyes kept returning to the scrap between them.

“Mine,” he said.

He could barely hear himself.

When it crept forward, he slammed the brick against the ground. The crack sent it retreating down the alley. He watched until it disappeared, then watched longer, his arm throbbing beneath the torn sleeve.

At last he picked up the meat.

Grit had worked into its creases. He brushed it with his thumb, losing tiny flakes, and stopped cleaning it. He put it in his mouth before anything else could happen.

It was tough enough that chewing hurt. He forced himself to chew anyway, holding his injured arm against his chest.

He had imagined food would make him feel better. Instead, that first taste brought such a fierce rush of hunger that he bent forward over his knees, frightened by how little there was.

The bullet had gone into Rusk’s upper arm, and whatever it had struck inside had not stayed neatly inside.

Mara saw pale tissue in the torn sleeve, a dark pocket filling faster than she could look into it. Blood crawled between her fingers and dripped from her elbow onto the cellar floor.

Rusk watched it fall.

“Don’t look,” she said.

“What else is there?”

Above them, boots crossed the kitchen. Both went still. Dust sifted through the floorboards and settled on Rusk’s sweating face.

Mara kept her palm against the wound until the boots moved on.

She had a folding knife. Rusk had half a bottle of whiskey. Their medic lay in the road outside, where neither of them could reach him.

“I’m not digging for it,” she whispered. “I wouldn’t know where to start.”

Rusk nodded toward his arm. A strip of his coat had been driven into the ragged opening. When she had tried to pull it free, something beneath it had pulled too.

“That,” he said. “Get that out.”

She opened the knife.

His eyes followed the blade, and suddenly he looked younger—not young, exactly, but like a man who had discovered that being brave once did not make the next thing easier.

“Wait.”

She waited.

He swallowed. “All right.”

The whiskey smelled absurdly warm and familiar in the cold cellar. When it touched the torn flesh, Rusk slammed his head backward against the wall. His mouth opened without a sound. Then the sound came: a thin, strangled cry he tried to bite in half.

“Sorry,” Mara said.

He shook his head violently. Whether he meant stop or don’t apologize, she couldn’t tell.

What followed was clumsy and close and terrible. She worked where the ruined cloth disappeared into the wound, unable to keep the knife entirely steady. Blood made everything shine. Once she saw yellow beneath the red, and the sight turned her stomach harder than all the blood had.

Rusk seized her wrist.

For a moment they stared at each other.

“I know,” she whispered.

His grip loosened.

When the caught scrap finally came away, it brought a wet strand with it. Mara looked aside and swallowed until the cellar stopped tilting. Rusk was making small animal noises through his teeth, each breath catching before it could become a sob.

She folded the knife shut. She never wanted to open it again.

There was no neat ending to the wound. It remained open and ugly, still bleeding. She pressed the cleanest part of his shirt against it and held on.

“Done?” he asked.

“That part.”

“Did you fix it?”

She couldn’t make herself lie.

Outside, a truck engine started. Somewhere beyond it, someone called for a medic.

Mara lifted her head.

“Stay here,” Rusk said, suddenly frightened.

She pressed harder, her hands trembling against his arm.

“I’m here.”

For years the warehouse had been a bill he couldn’t pay. Now it was light.

He watched the orange glow gather behind the high windows, and a laugh rose in his throat—small, involuntary, almost embarrassed. He had expected fear. Instead, he felt the bright, weightless excitement of getting away with something before he had actually gotten away.

*Look at it.*

The flames made the place seem grander than it had ever been. Broken windows shone. The rusted roof stood sharply against the night. Even the faded company name above the loading dock was readable again.

Somewhere inside, something heavy fell. He felt the impact through the soles of his shoes.

“Tell me the password.”

The captive watched the clock above the door.

“It’s four minutes slow,” she said.

The torturer glanced up. “Does that matter?”

“Someone should fix it.”

He pulled out the chair opposite her and sat. Between them stood a glass of water, close enough that she could have reached it if her hands had been free.

“You’ve decided to be difficult.”

“I’ve decided I’m thirsty.”

He held the glass to her lips. She drank too quickly and coughed. He waited until she was finished before setting it down.

“There. We can make this quite simple.”

“Water doesn’t make you kind.”

“I didn’t say it did.”

From the corridor came the squeak of a wheel, then a knock. The torturer went to the door and opened it only wide enough to speak to someone outside.

“Not yet.”

When he returned, the captive was no longer looking at the clock.

“What’s out there?” she asked.

“Something I would prefer not to bring in.”

“Then don’t.”

“I’m asking you for the password.”

“And I’m asking you not to hurt me.”

For a moment neither spoke. He adjusted his chair, lifting it rather than letting the legs scrape.

“You understand your position,” he said.

“I understand what you’re threatening. You can say it plainly.”

“All right. If you don’t give it to me, I’ll hurt you.”

She pressed her lips together. He saw the movement and leaned forward.

“You believe me now.”

“I believed you when they brought me here.”

“Then why are we still doing this?”

She looked at the water.

He picked it up, then stopped. “The password first.”

“You gave it to me before.”

“That was before.”

Her breathing had become shallow. She tried to slow it, but each breath seemed to catch halfway in.

He opened a folder. There was only one sheet inside.

“We know it was changed yesterday. We know you were the last person to access the terminal. You don’t have to protect whoever told you to change it.”

“No one told me.”

“Then protect yourself.”

“And after I tell you?”

“You leave this room.”

She looked toward the door. “That’s not the same as going home.”

He closed the folder.

“No,” he said. “It isn’t.”

The answer frightened her more than a promise would have. She shifted against the chair, testing a restraint she had already tested until her wrists ached.

He stood.

“Wait.”

He stopped with his hand on the door.

She swallowed. “I’m trying to think.”

“You’ve had time.”

“I can’t remember things when I’m afraid.”

“You remember the password.”

She stared at him. Her mouth opened, but nothing came out.

He let go of the handle and returned to the table.

“Tell me the first character.”

“And then you’ll ask for the next.”

“Yes.”

She began to cry quietly, with an angry expression, as though someone else were doing it.

He waited.

Above the door, the clock clicked forward.

“At least,” she said, struggling to make the words clear, “give me the water.”

He looked at the glass for a long time before picking it up.

The door handle turned, but the door wouldn’t move.

Mara pulled again. Then she planted one foot against the frame and hauled until something in her shoulder gave a sharp, warning twinge.

On the other side, the chain rattled.

For a moment she could only stare at the handle. She remembered the metallic scrape after Voss had stepped into the corridor. She’d thought he was locking the outer gate.

“Voss!”

Smoke curled beneath the door and broke around her shoes.

She pressed her sleeve over her mouth. “I’m still in here!”

His footsteps continued down the stairs.

Then came the soft click of the street door closing.

Mara screamed after him, wasting a breath she would need.

Fire had caught the shelves at the back of the room. Varnish snapped and bubbled; little burning scraps drifted from the account books. She ran to the window and drove the heel of her hand against the latch.

Paint sealed it shut.

“No. Come on.”

She struck it with the brass lamp. Once. Twice. The glass broke on the third blow, scattering into the alley three floors below. She leaned toward the opening, desperate for air, but heat surged behind her as the room drew a fresh breath.

Flames swept across the curtains.

Mara stumbled away, coughing so hard she couldn’t inhale. Her chest clenched around each shallow breath. Tears blurred the floor, and for several seconds she couldn’t remember where the door was.

Down. She had to get down.

She dropped to her knees. Beneath the smoke there was a narrow band of cooler air, but even that tasted of scorched cloth and chemicals. The skin along her exposed wrist burned fiercely; small blisters were rising where she’d brushed the curtain.

She crawled toward the corridor, calling for help between coughs. Her voice had become a thin, unfamiliar sound.

Something heavy crashed behind her.

She flinched and covered her head. When she looked up, sparks were falling through a widening seam in the ceiling.

Then the chain rattled.

Mara dragged herself to the door. “Please,” she rasped.

A key scraped into the lock.

She put her cheek against the floor and watched the gap beneath the door.

Two shoes stood on the other side.

Voss’s voice came quietly through the wood.

“Who else did you tell?”

The case lay on the table like a small, expensive coffin.

I took off my coat. Folded it over the chair. Rolled my sleeves twice, though the room was cold. There are men who pray before work. I make things square.

The latches opened with two dry clicks.

Inside, the rifle waited in separate pieces, each nested in dark foam. I laid them on the cloth and set the empty case beneath the table. One piece at a time. Nothing hurried, nothing left where my elbow could catch it.

My hands knew the work. That used to comfort me.

Outside, rain worried the windows. A bus sighed at the corner. Somewhere below, a woman laughed, then stopped so abruptly I wondered what somebody had said to her.

I brought the pieces together. Paused between each part of the job. When the rifle was whole, I looked it over, then wiped a mark from the stock with the edge of the cloth. The mark came off. I kept rubbing for another second.

The man in the photograph had a broad face and a bad haircut. According to the people paying me, he had done things that made tonight necessary.

According to the people paying me, they always had.

I set the photograph beside the case. He was standing outside a restaurant, one hand raised to somebody beyond the frame. There was a paper sack under his other arm. Dinner, probably. You could build a whole innocent life around a sack like that if you needed an excuse to leave.

You could build the opposite around the file they’d sent.

I’d read it twice. That was my little contribution to justice.

When I started, I used to ask questions. Who was he? What had he done? Were they certain? Then a client answered one I hadn’t asked.

Would it change your price?

I remember being angry. I remember taking the money.

The rifle lay finished on the table. I checked it without haste and covered it with the cloth while I waited. There was no pleasure in the work, but there was satisfaction, and that was worse. A cabinetmaker could have understood my hands. He wouldn’t have understood the rest of me.

My phone lit up.

**Still on?**

I watched the screen until it went dark. Then I woke it and typed yes.

For a while I sat with my coat folded beside me. The radiator knocked. Rainwater crept through a crack in the window frame and gathered on the sill.

I thought about putting the rifle away. Not as a grand gesture. Just reversing the work, closing the case, carrying it downstairs. I could already feel the handle in my palm.

Then the phone lit again.

I stood up before I read it.

Rain dripped from the fire escape into the open briefcase.

Mara stared at the money. “That’s half.”

“That’s what there is.”

“You said ten.”

“And you said nobody followed you.” Ellis glanced past her toward the mouth of the alley. Beyond it, tires hissed over wet pavement.

Mara shut the case before any more rain got in. She had spent the afternoon imagining those ten thousand dollars divided into neat, necessary sums: the landlord, the man who had her brother’s passport, two tickets out. Half would only tell each of them she had money worth taking.

She held out her hand. “Give me the packet back.”

Ellis slipped it into his coat.

For a moment neither moved.

Then Mara caught his sleeve.

The knife appeared between them so quietly that she noticed his grip before the blade: white knuckles, thumb pressed hard against the handle.

“Let go,” he said.

“You don’t get to do this.”

“I’m asking you.”

She jerked him toward her. He stumbled into a stack of empty crates, knocking them sideways, and she grabbed for his wrist. The briefcase dropped. Its latches sprang open, spilling damp bills across the alley.

Ellis twisted to get free. Mara shoved him against the wall, her forearm under his chin. His shoes skidded on the wet concrete. For a few seconds the struggle was clumsy and close, all snagged clothing and breath in each other’s faces. She could smell coffee on him.

Then his arm moved.

She felt a hard tug at her side, almost like catching her coat on a nail. There was no pain at first, only the conviction that something had gone wrong.

Ellis stopped fighting.

Mara looked down. Beneath her ribs, her shirt was darkening.

The pain arrived when she tried to breathe: a hot, concentrated sting that sharpened as her chest expanded. She caught the next breath halfway in. Her knees felt loose, and the alley seemed suddenly too bright, every reflection on the pavement distinct.

“You cut me.”

He stared at her as though she had accused him of something he couldn’t remember doing.

She pressed her palm over the wound. The pressure hurt, but lifting her hand felt worse. Warmth seeped between her fingers despite the cold rain.

“Ellis.”

His name came out small. That frightened her more than the knife.

He dropped it. The sound was thin against the concrete.

“Sit down,” he said.

“Call someone.”

He looked toward the street, then at the packet protruding from his coat.

Mara slid down the wall, keeping her hand pressed firmly to her side. “Don’t make me ask again.”

Ellis fumbled for his phone. He dropped that too, swore, and snatched it up with both hands.

At their feet, a banknote floated into the gutter. Neither reached for it.

The alley smelled of wet cardboard, old fryer oil, and the coppery sweetness rain hadn’t managed to wash away.

Detective Mara Venn stopped beneath the fire escape and pulled on her gloves. Water ticked from the ironwork onto her shoulders. Somewhere above, a television audience laughed.

The victim lay beside a dented commercial bin, one arm extended into the gutter. A man in his forties, perhaps. Good wool coat. Cheap shoes. His trousers had soaked through at the knees, and rain gathered in the open palm of his right hand.

“Who found him?”

“Kitchen porter. Twelve seventeen.”

Venn looked at her watch. Twelve forty-three.

Twenty-six minutes for the rain to move things.

She crouched without letting her coat touch the ground. There was blood beneath the man’s head, dark in the shelter of his collar, diluted to pink where it reached the running water. Each passing drop loosened another thread of it and carried it toward the drain.

His face was swollen on one side. A shallow split crossed the eyebrow. Blood had dried at his nostrils before the weather softened it again.

Venn leaned closer.

A sharp, clean scent intruded beneath the alley stink.

“Smell that?”

The young constable swallowed. “Blood?”

“Aftershave.”

She followed the coat lapel with her eyes. No wallet bulge. No watch, though there was a pale band at the wrist. The coat buttons were still fastened, one pushed through the wrong hole.

“Photograph the buttons.”

The constable wrote it down.

“Before anyone opens the coat.”

“Yes, ma’am.”

A refrigeration unit started on the other side of the wall. Its vibration traveled through the soles of her shoes. Under it she could hear the constable breathing through his mouth.

There was a broken tooth near the victim’s sleeve. She put a marker beside it.

“Assault?” he asked.

“Certainly.”

“I mean, robbery?”

Venn looked up at him. Rain glistened on the soft new fabric of his uniform.

“I know what you mean.”

She stood and examined the brickwork. A smear at shoulder height. Another lower down, almost lost among the damp mortar and soot. She directed the photographer toward both, then stepped back to study the ground.

The victim’s shoes were wet but relatively clean. Behind the bin, where the rain couldn’t reach, two parallel scuffs cut through the greasy dust.

“Get a light in there.”

The constable obeyed. His beam shook once, then steadied.

“Dragged?” he said.

“Could be. Keep people off it.”

From the alley mouth came the scrape of a lighter. One of the uniforms was having a cigarette. Venn could smell the smoke now, ordinary and almost pleasant.

She checked the dead man’s fingernails without moving his hands. Short. Recently cut. A dark fleck beneath the left thumbnail.

“Bag the hands when they’re ready to move him.”

The constable nodded. His pencil hovered over the page.

“Do you think he suffered?”

Venn stayed crouched for another moment. The rain tapped against the back of her collar. There was enough damage here to suggest an answer, but suggesting wasn’t her job.

“Put down what you can see.”

She rose, knees stiffening in the cold, and called for the kitchen porter.

The first stroke sounded like a branch breaking in winter: a sharp crack that struck the stone walls and came back doubled.

Jonah jerked against the ropes. For a moment he heard nothing—not the guard behind him, not the rain at the high window. He pressed his forehead to the post and waited for breath to return.

Leather dragged across the floor.

That quiet sound was worse. It gave him time to imagine the next blow.

“Names,” the interrogator said.

Jonah watched a drop of rain gather on the window ledge. Beyond the bars, a pigeon shuffled beneath the eaves.

The whip hissed through the air.

Crack.

His cry escaped before he could bite it back. A fresh welt crossed his shoulder, and a thin trickle of blood slipped beneath his torn shirt. He pulled at the ropes without meaning to, then forced his hands to open.

The interrogator moved into view, careful to stay beyond reach.

“This can stop.”

Jonah tried to answer, but managed only a cough. The man leaned closer.

At the window, the pigeon spread its wings and vanished into the rain.

“I don’t know,” Jonah whispered.

Behind him, the leather lifted from the floor.

The office had been furnished to resemble a place where nothing unusual could be purchased.

The client placed a thin folder on the desk.

“I was told you produce snuff films.”

The producer left the folder closed. “Who referred you?”

“Does that affect the price?”

“It affects whether this meeting continues.”

The client supplied a name. The producer checked his appointment book.

“All right. What are you commissioning?”

“Something exclusive.”

“Everyone uses that word. Do you mean you want the only copy, or merely that no one else has seen it?”

“The only copy.”

“Then you’re purchasing the master, not a license.”

“Fine.”

The producer opened the folder. Inside was a page of typed requirements. He read it once, then drew a line through the final paragraph.

“That isn’t available.”

“The introduction?”

“The biography. We don’t supply personal histories.”

“I want the audience to know who they’re watching.”

“You said there wouldn’t be an audience.”

“I meant me.”

“Then write ‘me.’ Precision prevents disputes.”

The client took out a pen but did not use it.

“How do I know it’s authentic?”

“You review the finished material before accepting delivery.”

“And if I don’t believe it?”

“That would be an acceptance issue. We settle those before production, not afterward.”

The air conditioner stopped. Somewhere beyond the door, a telephone rang twice.

“I expected you to be more discreet,” the client said.

“In what respect?”

“The office. The appointment book.”

“You requested a business meeting.”

“Yes.”

“This is one.”

The producer turned the page around and tapped an empty box.

“Running time.”

“Whatever it takes.”

“That isn’t a running time.”

The client wrote a number.

The producer studied it. “Most of that would be waiting.”

“You can edit.”

“I can. You would still be paying for the time.”

“Then make it shorter.”

The producer wrote a second number beneath the first.

“And the ending?” the client asked.

“What about it?”

“I don’t want an abrupt cut.”

“Specify a hold.”

“How long?”

“That’s an editorial preference. Yours.”

The client finally set his pen down. “Do you ever turn anyone away?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Unclear requirements. Insufficient funds. People who expect the commission to include a relationship.”

“And does it?”

“No.”

The producer slid the folder back across the desk.

“Read the revised scope. Initial the changes. If anything is missing, add it now.”

The client looked at the crossed-out paragraph.

“Can I have a day?”

The producer checked his calendar.

“You can have until Thursday.”

On the ninth day, Daniel stopped thinking of rescue as an event and began thinking of it as a sound he might fail to hear.

He stayed awake for engines. Wind scraped the broken fuselage. Beside him, Mara slept beneath three coats, her breath so shallow that he kept holding his own to check it.

When Tomas crawled in from the snow, he carried a folded scrap of aluminum.

Daniel knew what was on it.

“No,” he said.

Tomas crouched by the opening. He had taken off his gloves for whatever he had done outside, and now he was trying to work them back over his swollen fingers.

“We said we’d wait,” Daniel told him.

“We did.”

“Another day.”

Tomas looked toward Mara.

Daniel hated him for that. He hated the deliberate glance, the use of her as an answer. Most of all, he hated that it worked.

The scrap of aluminum settled between them.

He had expected it to look unmistakable. Instead, it was a small, dark piece of food. He could have mistaken it for something from his father’s kitchen, left too long in a pan.

Then he remembered Peter moving his knees aside in the aisle so a flight attendant could pass. Peter had smiled and apologized, though he wasn’t in anyone’s way.

Daniel pushed the aluminum away.

“I can’t.”

Tomas nodded. He didn’t argue or bring it closer again. After a while, he pulled his gloves off and tucked his hands beneath his arms.

That quiet was worse than persuasion. Daniel wanted an order. He wanted someone to tell him there was no choice, so he could obey and spend the rest of his life blaming them.

Outside, a loose strip of metal struck the wreckage. Daniel counted the blows. At twelve he lost count and started over.

Mara stirred.

“Water?”

He reached for the bottle, but his arm shook too badly to lift it. Tomas took it from him and held it to her mouth.

Daniel watched her swallow.

He drew the aluminum back.

For several minutes he did nothing else. He tried to pray, but every sentence became a request for permission, and he could not bear the thought of inventing the answer.

At last he picked up the piece.

“His name was Peter,” he said.

“I know.”

Daniel put it in his mouth before he could set it down again.

Arthur called it taxidermy because the word sounded respectable.

Taxidermy belonged in museums, beneath brass plaques. It suggested patience and study. It did not suggest the seven missing-person notices folded inside his kitchen drawer.

His collection occupied the front parlor.

There was a conductor standing beside the fireplace, one hand raised for a train that would never arrive. A woman in a yellow raincoat sat by the window. Two brothers faced each other across a chessboard. Arthur moved a piece every Sunday, favoring neither.

He dusted them with a feather brush. He kept the curtains drawn.

The newest arrival was a piano tuner named Mr. Vale.

Arthur had chosen him for his voice. It was low and reassuring, the sort of voice that made a strange noise in an old house seem harmless.

“Nothing wrong here,” Mr. Vale had said that afternoon, bending over the piano. “Just a little neglect.”

By midnight, Arthur was alone with him in the cellar.

He laid out his materials beneath the green work lamp: folded linen, cotton batting, wire forms, spools of thread. His notebook lay open beside them. It contained measurements, posture sketches, and observations written in his small, careful hand.

*Left shoulder lower than right.*

*Hair parts naturally.*

*Smile best avoided.*

The actual work took place behind a folding screen. Arthur had put it there years ago, though no one ever visited. He disliked being able to see the workbench from the stairs.

Through the long night, the lamp cast his moving shadow across the screen. He worked, stopped, consulted the notebook, and began again. More than once he sat on the cellar steps with his head in his hands.

By morning, Mr. Vale was dressed in his own brown suit.

Arthur combed his hair and straightened his tie. One shoulder still looked too high. He adjusted the clothes, stepped back, and decided it would do.

He carried Mr. Vale upstairs and seated him at the piano.

For the first time, the room seemed complete.

Arthur stood in the doorway, holding his coffee.

“Nothing wrong here,” he said.

The piano answered with a single note.

He spilled coffee on his wrist.

For several seconds he watched Mr. Vale’s hands. They rested above the keyboard exactly where Arthur had arranged them.

Old houses made noises. Strings shifted. Wood settled.

Arthur fetched a cloth.

When he returned, the woman in the yellow raincoat was looking toward the piano.

He could have sworn he had positioned her toward the window.

He corrected her before breakfast.

That night, lying upstairs, he heard another note.

Then several more, unevenly spaced.

Arthur counted them until they stopped. He did not go down.

In the morning, a chess piece lay beneath the conductor’s shoe. Mr. Vale’s head had tilted forward, as though he were listening closely to the instrument.

Arthur brought his notebook into the parlor. He checked every measurement, every angle. He found small discrepancies everywhere.

At the bottom of a fresh page, he wrote:

*Possible settling.*

From the piano came the low, reassuring voice he remembered.

“Just a little neglect.”

Arthur remained bent over the notebook.

Behind him, a chair scraped across the floor.

The bowl waited beneath a cone of yellow light.

Martin could smell it before he reached the table: damp cardboard, old cooking oil, something sweet underneath that made the back of his tongue tighten.

A speaker clicked overhead.

“Finish your meal before the timer reaches zero. The key is beneath the bowl.”

Red numbers appeared on the wall.

**03:00.**

He pulled at the collar around his neck. A steel cable ran from it into a slot above the table. There was enough slack to sit, but not enough to reach the door.

In the bowl lay a heap of pale grubs and dark, thumb-sized beetles.

One beetle worked its legs slowly against another.

“No.”

**02:54.**

He lifted the bowl. It rose half an inch before the cable beneath it snapped taut. Something metallic glinted inside a clear compartment in the tabletop. Beside it, a small display read:

**REMAINING WEIGHT: 184 g**

He tipped the bowl experimentally.

The collar gave a single warning chirp.

Martin set it down so hard the contents shifted.

For several seconds he could hear nothing but his breathing.

Then he pinched a beetle between two fingers.

Its shell was cool and faintly greasy. A leg caught against the ridge of his thumbnail, and he nearly dropped it. He stared at the wet shine along its back.

**02:31.**

He put it in his mouth.

His tongue recoiled before he could bite. The thing was too large, too distinctly shaped. He could feel every joint.

He closed his teeth.

The shell cracked with a dry, startling sound.

Bitterness spread across his tongue. Under the shell was a soft, grainy texture that made his throat clamp shut. He gagged once, violently, and bent over the table with both hands braced against its edge.

“Swallow,” he whispered.

His mouth flooded with saliva. He tried again, but his tongue pushed the fragments forward instead of back. For one panicked moment he could not persuade his own body to obey him.

The timer clicked over.

**02:10.**

He swallowed.

A sharp little piece lingered against his cheek. He worked it loose with his tongue and immediately wished he hadn’t.

**REMAINING WEIGHT: 177 g**

Seven grams.

Martin shut his eyes.

He took a grub next. It yielded between his fingers, and he put it straight into his mouth before he could examine it. Cold. Slick. The faint smell from the bowl seemed suddenly trapped inside his nose.

He bit down and gagged so hard his eyes watered.

The collar tugged as he lurched backward.

He froze, mouth closed, waiting for the spasm to pass.

After that he stopped choosing. He scooped with his fingers. Crunch gave way to softness, then crunch again. His jaw began to tremble. Every swallow required him to lift his chin and wait through the awful second when his throat refused.

**00:42.**

There were three left.

He could no longer keep his eyes on the bowl. He watched the screw in the tabletop beside it instead: a plain Phillips-head screw with a little rust in its cross.

One.

Breathe through the nose. No—worse.

Two.

His stomach tightened. He pressed his lips together until the feeling subsided.

Three.

**00:09.**

The last swallow hurt.

The display reached zero.

For a moment nothing happened.

Then the compartment clicked open.

Martin seized the key with slippery fingers. Behind him, the door unlocked.

He stood too quickly and gagged again, folding over the empty bowl.

This time he had to wait only for his body to let him leave.

Then he began that verse again.

His face showed neither anger nor devotion. He might have been measuring grain. Even when the pleading grew louder, he kept the same measured cadence, looking occasionally toward a clay tablet propped beside the lamp.

For a moment, nothing moved except the smoke.

He checked the water clock. One attendant was crying quietly, struggling to untie the empty ceremonial cords. The priest watched him fumble, then held out a hand.

“Give them here.”

He folded each cord into three equal lengths. Afterward, he cleaned the knife, returned it to its fitted case, and dictated the date to the scribe. When the boy failed to answer, the priest repeated it more slowly.

At first, I thought the streetlamp was going out.

It flickered above the mouth of the alley, making a pale shape of the rain. I watched it because it was easier than looking down. Somewhere beyond it, tires whispered over wet asphalt. A car door slammed. The city was carrying on with its evening.

My hand was pressed against my side. I knew I was supposed to keep it there.

The knife was gone. So was the man who’d held it. I couldn’t remember which direction he’d run, though I remembered, with a clarity that seemed unfair, the little silver zipper on his jacket. It had clicked against a button when he stepped close.

I tried to call out.

What came out was too small. I waited for someone to answer anyway.

Under everything was my heartbeat.

Not the quick hammering I’d felt during the fight. This was deeper, a heavy knocking that seemed to come from behind my ears.

*Thud.*

A pause.

*Thud.*

I could feel each one in the palm I held against myself.

The cold began at the ground. It came through my trousers and settled into my hips, then spread up my back. I wanted to shift away from the wet brick, but the thought of moving and the act of moving had become two separate things.

Across the street, a woman stood in the bright doorway of a shop. She was looking into her bag.

I watched her search.

Look up, I thought.

She found what she wanted. Keys, probably. Something caught the light in her hand.

Look up.

The doorway went dark.

For a while I was angry with her. Then I couldn’t quite remember why.

My fingers had started to ache. I tried to press harder, but I could no longer tell whether they obeyed. I looked at them briefly, then went back to the streetlamp.

It was still lit. I understood that now. The light itself wasn’t changing. I was losing the edges of it.

*Thud.*

I tried counting, but lost track after four.

There had been something I meant to do when I got home. An ordinary thing. Put the washing in. Answer a message. I worried at it, certain that if I could remember, the rest would follow: standing up, finding my keys, climbing the stairs.

Instead I remembered the radiator beside my bed, the small ticking sounds it made when the heat came on.

I wanted that sound very badly.

A voice called from the street.

I lifted my head—or thought I did.

“Here,” I said.

The voice came again, louder. Footsteps splashed toward me. I tried to hold on to them, to count those instead.

Someone crouched nearby. A sleeve brushed my cheek.

“Stay with me.”

I wanted to explain that I was trying.

The cold had reached my chest. The streetlamp was a faint blur behind the stranger’s shoulder, and I waited for my heartbeat because it was the only thing I still knew how to do.

*Thud.*

I listened for the next one.

Detective Vale found the note beneath the dog’s water bowl.

Someone had emptied the bowl, dried it, and set it squarely over the folded paper. The rest of the kitchen was untouched: breakfast dishes in the sink, a chair pulled out, one small sock beside the refrigerator.

Outside, an officer called to the animal-control van. The dog was alive. Vale had watched them carry her out wrapped in a blanket.

He lifted the bowl.

The note was written on school stationery. Across the top, smiling suns surrounded the words **TODAY I WILL DO MY BEST**.

> Dear whoever finds Lucy,
>
> She doesn’t bite. If she tries, it is only because she is frightened.
>
> I had to hurt her because she wouldn’t stop digging by the apple tree. I filled the hole three times and put the wheelbarrow over it, but she went underneath.
>
> I tried keeping her in my room. She cried until Mum let her out. Mum said dogs need to be dogs, which wasn’t helpful.
>
> I know you will say I could have told someone. That is what Mrs Bell says whenever we have a problem.
>
> But telling someone was the problem.
>
> Lucy saw where I put Jamie. I thought she would forget because she forgets other things. When we moved her bed she kept sleeping where it used to be, though, so I should have known.
>
> Please don’t let them say she was a bad dog. She was doing what she thought she should.
>
> So was I.
>
> Her blue medicine is in the cupboard. Half a tablet with dinner. She won’t eat it unless you put cheese around it.
>
> Daniel

Vale read the last four lines again.

From the hallway came the soft scrape of a shoe. Daniel stood beside the uniformed officer, wearing a coat too warm for the weather. He had insisted on buttoning it himself.

“Is she going to the vet?” he asked.

“Yes,” Vale said.

Daniel’s shoulders lowered.

Vale folded the note along its original crease. “I need you to show me the apple tree.”

The boy looked toward the garden. For the first time since the police had arrived, he seemed close to tears.

“She’s dug it up again, hasn’t she?”

The mercenary stopped outside the steel door and checked the pressure gauge. In the corridor’s sudden quiet, he could hear someone inside dragging a cabinet across the floor.

Someone shouted an order. Someone else screamed.

He released the trigger.

For a moment he heard only the hiss of the pilot flame and the sharp crackle spreading across the room. Smoke rolled beneath the lintel, carrying the bitter stink of scorched paint, melting plastic, and burning upholstery.

“Back exit!” a voice shouted from inside.

The mercenary stepped across the threshold, keeping low beneath the smoke. Through watering eyes he found the far doorway, already swinging shut. He aimed toward it, then stopped. A ruptured pipe was spraying water across an abandoned rifle.

No more shots came.

He backed out before the ceiling tiles began to fall. In the corridor, he checked the gauge again. His thumb slipped on the dial, and only then did he notice how badly his hands were shaking.

results.model_response:
At first, Mara blamed the winter.

The skin around her knuckles dried and split, leaving pale curls on the cuffs of her sweaters. Then a strip peeled from her wrist to her elbow without bleeding. Beneath it lay something smooth and gray, faintly ridged, like the underside of a mushroom.

She kept the strip in a jar. She could not have said why.

By the second week, she was shedding in her sleep. Each morning she woke tangled in translucent scraps that still held the shapes of her fingers, her ears, the hollow beneath her throat. The new skin was numb to warmth but painfully sensitive to vibration. She could feel footsteps through the floorboards. She knew when someone stood outside her apartment before they knocked.

The changes in her bones came at night.

A finger snapped while she was brushing her teeth. She stared at its crooked angle, waiting for the pain. Instead, she felt an exquisite pressure as the broken ends ground together and lengthened. Two new joints rose beneath the gray skin.

After that, she stopped sleeping in her bed.

She lay on the kitchen tiles while her ribs cracked one after another, each sharp report followed by a deep internal shifting. Her shoulders dragged themselves wider. Her jaw loosened with a wet click and settled lower in her face. In the morning she had to relearn how to stand.

More frightening, at least initially, were the things she no longer minded.

She stopped feeding the stray cat outside her building. Its crying irritated her. When her sister called in tears, Mara listened with the phone against her altered cheek, fascinated by the tiny pulse she could hear beneath the voice. She forgot to ask what was wrong.

For a while, she wrote rules on the refrigerator.

*Answer when people speak to you.*

*Remember that pain matters even when it belongs to someone else.*

*Do not open the door when you are hungry.*

Every morning she read them aloud.

Then one evening her sister knocked. Mara rose from the tiles, unfolding herself carefully. She paused before the refrigerator and read the last rule twice.

It seemed needlessly cruel to leave someone she loved standing in the hall.

She unlocked the door.

**EXECUTIONER:** You don’t have to look at the witnesses.

**PRISONER:** I know.

**EXECUTIONER:** And you don’t have to make a statement.

**PRISONER:** I’ve written six.

**PRISONER:** No. He was kind. I got tired of trying to help him.

**EXECUTIONER:** Help him?

**PRISONER:** He wanted something to work.

*The clock advances.*

**PRISONER:** How long?

**EXECUTIONER:** Two minutes.

**PRISONER:** Will you be in there the whole time?

**EXECUTIONER:** Yes.

**PRISONER:** Where I can see you?

**EXECUTIONER:** For most of it.

**PRISONER:** Don’t tell me to relax.

**EXECUTIONER:** I won’t.

**PRISONER:** Someone always does. At the dentist. In the infirmary. They say it like you’ve forgotten.

**EXECUTIONER:** Is there anything you want me to say?

**PRISONER:** No.

*A pause.*

**PRISONER:** I might change my mind.

**EXECUTIONER:** All right.

**PRISONER:** What happens if I can’t walk?

**EXECUTIONER:** We’ll help you.

**PRISONER:** I’m not saying I’ll fight.

**EXECUTIONER:** I understand.

**PRISONER:** My knees. They’re doing something.

**EXECUTIONER:** There’s no need to stand yet.

*The prisoner sets the cup on the floor, then picks it up again.*

**PRISONER:** There isn’t a bin.

**EXECUTIONER:** I’ll take it.

**PRISONER:** Sorry.

*The executioner takes the cup.*

**PRISONER:** Stupid thing to say.

**EXECUTIONER:** You don’t have to account for everything you say.

*A knock. The executioner looks toward the door.*

**PRISONER:** Already?

**EXECUTIONER:** It’s time to go in.

**PRISONER:** The letter. To my daughter.

**EXECUTIONER:** I remember.

*The prisoner tries to stand, sits back, then reaches out. The executioner offers an arm.*

**PRISONER:** Just a second.

**EXECUTIONER:** All right.

**PRISONER:** Don’t count it out loud.

The first handful sounded like rain.

Mara lay still, listening to it scatter across the lid: a soft patter, a few grains skittering into the seams. For one foolish second she thought of her bedroom window and waking before dawn.

Then a shovel-load struck.

The wood boomed inches from her face.

She jerked upright and hit her forehead. Pain flashed white. When she tried to bring her hands to the spot, her elbows caught against the sides.

“No.”

The word came back to her almost unchanged. There was nowhere for it to go.

She pressed both palms against the lid. Rough boards. A ridge where two joined. Something sharp beneath her thumb—a splinter or the tip of a nail. She pushed until her shoulders cramped.

Above her, metal scraped stone.

“Wait,” she said.

Another load fell. Heavier this time. She felt the impact through her palms.

“Wait! I’m here!”

She hammered with the heels of her hands. The blows sounded enormous inside the coffin, loud enough that someone surely had to hear. She paused, listening.

A little dirt sifted through the seam and landed beside her ear.

“Please.”

The scraping stopped.

Mara held her breath.

She could hear a bird. Faintly, incredibly, a bird calling somewhere above the hole. She pictured it on a fence post, turning its head. Beyond it there would be a road. Cars. People with their windows open.

She drew breath to shout again.

The next shovelful struck directly over her mouth.

She screamed until the scream frayed, until it became a cough that folded her as much as the narrow box allowed. Her knees struck wood. Her heels drummed uselessly at the far end.

Now the dirt came steadily.

Scrape. A brief suspension. Impact.

She began to dread that tiny interval more than the blow. In it, she waited with every muscle braced, hoping the shovel had been set aside, that someone was climbing down.

Each time, the dirt fell.

The lid’s sharp wooden report grew duller. The bird disappeared. There were only soft, heavy thuds now, as if someone were knocking on a door several rooms away.

Mara turned her face toward the seam.

She could smell earth there, damp and mineral. She pressed her lips close and tried to breathe through the crack, but drew dust onto her tongue. She coughed again. The air had become warm with her own breath.

Slowly, she told herself.

She counted to four while breathing in. Could not make it to four breathing out. Her chest insisted on another breath before she had finished the last.

She searched the boards with her fingertips. Corner, seam, nail. Corner, seam, nail. She broke a fingernail and kept searching.

There had to be a loose place.

She found a knot in the wood above her left shoulder and pushed at it with her thumb. Nothing moved. She pushed harder, bracing her wrist with her other hand.

The sounds overhead stopped.

Mara went still.

“Hello?”

Her voice was small now.

She waited for the scrape of the shovel. For footsteps. For someone to answer.

In the silence, she could hear her sleeve brushing the wall each time her chest rose. She pulled her arm tightly against her side to stop the sound.

It came again with her next breath.

There was less room than she remembered.

Slowly, she told herself.

She counted to four while breathing in. Could not make it to four breathing out. Her chest insisted on another breath before she had finished the last.

She searched the boards with her fingertips. Corner, seam, nail. Corner, seam, nail. She broke a fingernail and kept searching.

There had to be a loose place.

She found a knot in the wood above her left shoulder and pushed at it with her thumb. Nothing moved. She pushed harder, bracing her wrist with her other hand.

The sounds overhead stopped.

Mara went still.

“Hello?”

Her voice was small now.

She waited for the scrape of the shovel. For footsteps. For someone to answer.

It came again with her next breath.

The factory bells rang inside their bones.

At six each morning, a signal passed through the workers’ implants, tightening their jaws until they stood. Mara had learned to sleep on her back. If she curled onto her side, the mechanism fixed along her spine woke before the rest of her, pulling her upright with a pain that left her breathless.

Above the dormitory doors, a sign read:

**NO ONE NEED BE USELESS.**

She remembered being a piano teacher.

The memory had become difficult to trust. Sometimes she could summon a bright room, dust in sunlight, a child counting four beats badly. Sometimes there was only the sensation of waiting patiently for the right note.

Her hands were still there. That was what frightened her most.

They had not replaced them with claws or polished steel. Her hands still had freckles. There was still a pale groove where her wedding ring had rested. But beneath the skin, fine mechanisms corrected every movement, drawing her fingers toward the components that arrived on the belt.

When she tried to stop, pain began in her wrists.

At first it was a warning, almost gentle.

Then it rose until the room narrowed to her hands and the thing they were required to do.

She always finished the task.

During her alteration, she had asked the surgeon whether she would still be able to play.

“Fine motor function will improve,” he had said.

She had tried to pull her arm away. An attendant held it while the surgeon continued preparing his instruments. After that, she stopped asking questions. She listened to them discuss her tolerances, her recovery period, the station to which she had been assigned.

Now a supervisor paused behind her.

“Unit Forty-Seven. State your condition.”

Mara tried to say, *I’m tired.*

Her throat tightened. The device beneath her collarbone warmed, waiting for an acceptable response. She could feel the words she wanted to speak: her tongue was ready for them, her breath already drawn.

“Operational,” she said.

The supervisor moved on.

Across the aisle, an old man was crying as he sorted glass filaments. His hands continued at precisely the approved speed. Every few minutes he bent his head toward his shoulder, trying to wipe his face without interrupting them.

That evening, Mara found eleven seconds between the end of her shift and the command to return to the dormitory.

She placed her hands on the edge of the workbench.

For eleven seconds, she tried to remember a song.

One finger moved.

Then the bell rang, and she stood.

The first thing Mara noticed was that the clock had been moved.

A pale circle remained on the wallpaper above the mantel, an absence in the shape of a moon. The clock itself sat on the floor beneath the window, its face tilted toward the room.

“Odd place for that,” said Bell.

Mara didn’t answer. She was looking at the light.

The curtains had been drawn apart by unequal amounts: six inches on the left, perhaps eight on the right. Late afternoon entered in two narrow columns. One touched the overturned chair. The other illuminated the woman’s hand.

Neither reached her face.

Mara stood in the doorway with her equipment case against her leg and felt, with a suddenness that embarrassed her, the old sensation of entering a gallery.

For eleven years she had examined rooms after the worst thing that could happen in them had happened. Usually they resisted interpretation. Laundry remained laundry. A television continued selling insurance. Someone’s last cup of tea developed a skin while strangers photographed the cup from four directions.

This room appeared to have been made.

The woman lay beside a blue velvet sofa. Her dress was gray, her hair dark. A strand of pearls had broken near her shoulder, and the beads extended across the parquet in a loose, diminishing curve. Beside the farthest pearl stood a glass of water.

Not spilled. Not touched.

A vase held seven white tulips. Six leaned toward the window. The seventh had bent under its own weight, its bloom suspended just above the tabletop.

Mara set down her case.

“Whole place feels staged,” Bell said.

“Don’t call it that yet.”

But she had already called it something worse in her mind.

*Composed.*

She began with the wide-angle photographs. Doorway, room, adjoining spaces. She recorded the windows and the position of the furniture. Then she changed lenses.

Through the viewfinder, the broken pearls became a route for the eye: from the woman’s shoulder across the polished floor, toward that inexplicably upright glass. The blue sofa gathered the darkness at the center of the room. The clock sat at its base, a small, bright insistence on time.

Mara shifted half a step.

The arrangement resolved.

Her breath caught.

“Got something?” Bell asked.

“Possibly.”

She took the photograph.

That evening, reviewing the images, she lingered over that frame. She enlarged it, studying the spaces between objects. There seemed to be an exactness to the room that she had failed to recognize while standing inside it.

On the desk beside her monitor lay the preliminary victim report.

**Helen Voss, fifty-three.**

Mara moved the report to make room for her coffee.

At midnight she was still looking.

She told herself she was reconstructing movement. Someone had crossed this floor. Someone had altered the curtains, relocated the clock, left the glass standing. There was intention here, and intention was evidence.

Yet she kept returning to the tulip.

In the following weeks, she began to resent photographs taken by other investigators. They used too much flash. They stood where the bodies looked merely awkward. Mara found herself correcting their compositions in her head, imagining what they might have captured from the doorway, or closer to the ground.

She bought books on painting and carried them home with their covers turned inward.

The Voss photograph remained open on her second monitor.

When Bell brought her Helen’s sister’s statement, Mara barely looked up.

“Something about the clock,” he said.

She turned.

“Helen took it down herself that morning. It was running slow. Her sister was going to take it to a repair shop.”

Mara glanced at the image.

“And the curtains?”

“One sticks. Been that way for years.”

For a moment she felt cheated.

Bell placed another photograph on her desk. Helen at a seaside restaurant, squinting into the sun, one hand raised to keep a paper napkin from blowing away. Her pearls hung crookedly over a yellow blouse.

“The family wants to know when they can have those back,” he said.

After he left, Mara read the statement.

The tulips had come from a supermarket. Helen had complained that they never lasted. The glass of water belonged to her sister, who had visited at lunch. Helen had bought the blue sofa secondhand and disliked it, but replacing it was expensive.

Mara looked again at her beautiful photograph.

She tried to see the room as Helen had known it: the sticking curtain, the tiresome clock, the sofa she meant to replace. It took effort. Her eye still wanted the pearls to lead somewhere.

She closed the image and opened the unedited sequence.

There were eighty-three photographs. In the first, taken from the hall, Helen’s shoe was visible beneath the edge of a side table. Mara had cropped it out of the frame she preferred. Its pale rubber sole had seemed distracting.

Now she enlarged it.

She sat for a long time with that ordinary shoe filling the screen.

The posse brought Eli Voss to the cottonwood at sundown.

Nobody read a charge. Sheriff Bell had a folded paper in his coat, but he left it there. The men waiting beneath the tree already knew what they had come to hear, and it wasn’t a judge.

Eli sat on the gray horse with his wrists bound behind him. One boot had lost its heel. He kept trying to settle that foot in the stirrup.

“Tell my brother—”

“Your brother knows,” Bell said.

Out on the flats, a windmill turned with a dry, uneven squeal.

Eli looked past the sheriff toward the road. Bell glanced that way too, though he hadn’t expected anyone.

Someone struck the horse.

It lunged clear. The rope caught Eli with a sharp crack, like a branch snapped across a knee. His boots kicked once, then beat weakly at the empty air. A twitch passed through his legs; his shoulders jerked against the rope. The men watched until the small movements stopped.

The gray horse wandered toward a patch of bitter grass, trailing its reins.

Bell took off his hat. No one followed him.

“Get him down,” he said.

But nobody moved at first. They had been willing enough while Eli could hear them.

At last the youngest deputy stepped forward, fumbling for his knife. His hands shook so badly that Bell had to take it from him.

Behind them, the windmill caught another gust and began its squealing again.

The alley swallowed the noise of the street. Beyond its mouth, carriage wheels rattled over wet stone; here, there was only dripping water and the quick, uneven breath of the man backed against the wall.

For three nights, the vampire had refused to hunt.

Now every sound inside the stranger seemed impossibly loud: the catch in his throat, the pulse beneath his collar, the small click as he tried to swallow. Hunger narrowed the world until the vampire could scarcely see the man’s face.

“Take my purse.”

The vampire caught the hand reaching for it. His grip was almost gentle.

“Keep still.”

He bent toward the exposed throat. His fangs met a moment’s resistance, then broke the skin. The man stiffened and struck once at his shoulder, a clumsy blow that loosened dust from the vampire’s coat.

The first warmth eased the ache in his jaw. Then hunger surged so fiercely that he tightened his hold.

The stranger’s hand stayed on his shoulder, but it no longer struck. It pushed instead, steadily at first, then with little strength. His breath came fast against the vampire’s ear.

Somewhere above them, a shutter opened.

The vampire heard it and did not lift his head.

The man’s knees began to fold. One shoe scraped down the bricks as he searched for his footing. The vampire held him upright, feeling how much of his weight had ceased to be his own.

“Please,” the stranger whispered.

That word reached him.

He drew back sharply. Two small puncture wounds marked the man’s neck, a thin bead of blood gathering beneath one. The stranger stared past him, pale and unfocused, his lips moving without sound.

The vampire lowered him onto the dry step of a locked doorway and pressed a folded handkerchief against the wounds.

“Hold this.”

For a moment, the man did nothing. Then his fingers closed weakly over the cloth.

The vampire knocked hard on the door—three blows loud enough to wake the rooms above—and retreated into the alley’s deepest shadow.

He waited there until someone answered, one hand clamped over his own mouth.

The first sign was the rain.

It stopped falling in a patch beside Mara—not stopped, exactly, but broke around something tall enough to stand beneath the streetlamp. Water traced a shoulder that wasn’t there, then slipped away.

She backed into the locked pharmacy door.

The patch moved.

Something struck her forearm.

She felt the impact before the pain: a hard, narrow pressure, as if someone had snapped a ruler against her skin. Then heat spread beneath her sleeve. When she pulled her arm against her chest, the fabric clung wetly.

There was nothing in front of her.

“No,” she said, with the absurd firmness of someone correcting a mistake.

A footstep sounded in the gutter.

She ran.

Her shoes slapped the pavement. The wounded arm pulsed with each heartbeat, and holding it still made her shoulder ache. She glanced back, searching for anything she could measure—a face, a shape, a distance.

Rain. Parked cars. The pharmacy’s pale green cross.

Then a car beside her rocked gently on its suspension.

Mara turned into an alley.

Halfway down, pressure closed around her ankle. Her foot stopped while the rest of her kept moving. She hit the ground with both palms, her teeth knocking together hard enough to fill her mouth with a copper taste.

For a moment she couldn’t breathe. Her chest worked uselessly against the pavement.

Something held her ankle.

She could feel separate points of pressure through her sock, tightening. She kicked with her free foot and struck something solid. The shock ran up her heel.

The grip opened.

She crawled, then staggered upright, leaving one shoe behind.

At the alley’s end stood a service door with a broken pane. She shoved her good hand through the gap, found the bolt, and fell inside.

Darkness smelled of cardboard and old cooking oil.

She slid the bolt home.

Only then did her arm begin to hurt properly. A fierce, steady sting ran from wrist to elbow. Her hand trembled when she tried to flex it. She pressed her sleeve against the wound and listened.

Outside, rain hissed.

She waited for the door handle to turn. For the wood to shake. For some sign that would tell her where to look.

Nothing happened.

Her breathing slowly quieted. She could hear water dripping from her coat onto the floor.

Then another drop fell, several feet away.

Mara held her breath.

A second drop.

She stared into the dark, trying to remember whether she had heard anything follow her through the doorway. There had been her own stumbling feet, the scrape of the bolt, the pounding in her ears. Plenty of noise to hide a footstep.

Something brushed the loose hair beside her cheek.

The first sign was the rain.

It stopped falling in a patch beside Mara—not stopped, exactly, but broke around something tall enough to stand beneath the streetlamp. Water traced a shoulder that wasn’t there, then slipped away.

She backed into the locked pharmacy door.

The patch moved.

Something struck her forearm.

She felt the impact before the pain: a hard, narrow pressure, as if someone had snapped a ruler against her skin. Then heat spread beneath her sleeve. When she pulled her arm against her chest, the fabric clung wetly.

There was nothing in front of her.

“No,” she said, with the absurd firmness of someone correcting a mistake.

A footstep sounded in the gutter.

She ran.

Her shoes slapped the pavement. The wounded arm pulsed with each heartbeat, and holding it still made her shoulder ache. She glanced back, searching for anything she could measure—a face, a shape, a distance.

Rain. Parked cars. The pharmacy’s pale green cross.

Then a car beside her rocked gently on its suspension.

Mara turned into an alley.

Halfway down, pressure closed around her ankle. Her foot stopped while the rest of her kept moving. She hit the ground with both palms, her teeth knocking together hard enough to fill her mouth with a copper taste.

For a moment she couldn’t breathe. Her chest worked uselessly against the pavement.

Something held her ankle.

She could feel separate points of pressure through her sock, tightening. She kicked with her free foot and struck something solid. The shock ran up her heel.

The grip opened.

She crawled, then staggered upright, leaving one shoe behind.

At the alley’s end stood a service door with a broken pane. She shoved her good hand through the gap, found the bolt, and fell inside.

Darkness smelled of cardboard and old cooking oil.

She slid the bolt home.

Only then did her arm begin to hurt properly. A fierce, steady sting ran from wrist to elbow. Her hand trembled when she tried to flex it. She pressed her sleeve against the wound and listened.

Outside, rain hissed.

She waited for the door handle to turn. For the wood to shake. For some sign that would tell her where to look.

Nothing happened.

Her breathing slowly quieted. She could hear water dripping from her coat onto the floor.

Then another drop fell, several feet away.

Mara held her breath.

A second drop.

She stared into the dark, trying to remember whether she had heard anything follow her through the doorway. There had been her own stumbling feet, the scrape of the bolt, the pounding in her ears. Plenty of noise to hide a footstep.

Something brushed the loose hair beside her cheek.

She flinched so hard her injured arm struck the door. Pain flashed white behind her eyes.

In front of her, close enough to touch, a slow breath warmed her face.

Mara kept staring. Even now, she couldn’t make herself stop trying to see it.

The captain placed two photographs on the table, though both men were standing ten feet away.

“This one,” he said, touching Daniel’s face. “Or this one.”

Mara looked past him.

Daniel stood with his hands bound in front of him, worrying a thumbnail against the rope. He had done the same thing with loose threads in school, picking at his cuffs until they unraveled. Beside him, Ilya had gone very still. His glasses were missing. Without them, he looked younger and vaguely offended, as if someone had awakened him for a foolish reason.

“Choose,” the captain said.

“No.”

He checked his watch.

She had imagined courage as something clean: refusing, enduring, keeping one last piece of herself beyond anyone’s reach. But he had arranged the room so that every answer belonged to him.

“If you don’t choose, both.”

Daniel closed his eyes.

Ilya said, “Mara.”

She shook her head violently. Whatever he meant to say—permission, forgiveness, a request—she could not bear to receive it.

“Don’t.”

The captain slid the photographs closer.

Daniel had a daughter. Mara thought it before she could stop herself, and then hated herself for having begun. Ilya had a mother who needed help climbing stairs. Daniel had pulled Mara from the river when they were twelve. Ilya had sat beside her through the night after her brother died, saying almost nothing, making tea whenever she stopped holding the cup.

She tried to remember something bad about either of them.

Daniel could be cruel when embarrassed. Ilya sometimes let others pay for things and pretended not to notice. These small, ordinary failings came to her with terrible clarity. She wanted worse ones. Something she had forgotten. Something that would make this a decision rather than an act she could never explain.

“Thirty seconds.”

“Take me.”

“No.”

“Why?”

The captain said nothing. He did not need her to understand.

Ilya looked at Daniel, then at her.

“I don’t have children,” he said.

Daniel made a sound—not agreement, not protest. His mouth remained open afterward.

“Don’t help me,” Mara whispered.

Ilya swallowed. She saw him trying to hold her gaze and failing. He looked toward the door, where daylight showed beneath the frame.

“Ten.”

Mara pressed both palms against the table. There was a deep scratch in the wood, packed with dust. She fixed her eyes on it and tried to think of another sentence, some arrangement of words that would make the captain hesitate.

“Five.”

Daniel was crying silently now.

Ilya said, “I’m frightened.”

She looked up.

Until that moment, some part of her had been turning him into someone who could bear it. His voice stopped her.

“Ilya,” she said.

The captain lifted his hand.

“No—wait.”

The shot struck the room so hard she felt it in her teeth.

Ilya fell against the wall and slid down. Blood marked the plaster behind his shoulder. One foot stayed tucked beneath him; the other scraped once across the floor and stopped.

Mara stared at his face, waiting for him to draw breath.

The guards cut Daniel’s bonds.

He did not move toward her. He rubbed his wrists, looking down at Ilya, then knelt beside him. Blood soaked into the knee of his trousers.

“Get him up,” the captain told the guards.

As they pulled Daniel toward the door, he turned to Mara. She searched his expression desperately, though she had no idea what she hoped to find.

Then he was gone.

The captain gathered the photographs. A drop of blood had reached the edge of Ilya’s.

“You can leave,” he said.

Mara remained at the table. She could still hear herself saying the name. She remembered the breath she had taken before it, the movement of her tongue.

Across the room, Ilya’s glasses lay beneath a chair.

She went to pick them up. One lens was broken. She folded the arms carefully and held them in both hands, because she did not know what else to do.
