The first thing Daniel noticed was the smell of bleach.

Not because it was strong, but because it was always there.

It drifted through the hedge when his neighbor watered the roses. It clung to the casserole Martin brought over after Daniel’s divorce. Even the borrowed hedge trimmer came back smelling faintly of a public swimming pool.

“Can’t stand a dirty tool,” Martin had said.

For three years, Daniel had mistaken this for a virtue.

Then Martin went away for the weekend and asked him to feed the cat.

“Food’s in the pantry. She hides, so don’t worry if you don’t see her.”

On Saturday evening, Daniel heard scratching beneath the kitchen floor.

He called the cat’s name. The scratching stopped, then resumed at the basement door.

The key Martin had given him opened the front door but not that one. Daniel might have left it alone if something hadn’t knocked against the other side—three quick, hollow taps.

He found a screwdriver in a drawer.

The latch was cheap. That bothered him later: how little effort it took to enter the worst place he would ever see.

At the bottom of the stairs, he found a washing machine, a workbench, and a chest freezer humming beneath a calendar. The cat slipped past his ankles and fled upstairs.

He should have followed it.

Instead, he noticed the second door.

It stood open an inch. Beyond it was warm light and what looked like a row of framed photographs.

Daniel pushed.

For a moment, his mind insisted he had found a hobby room.

There were glass cabinets. Small brass labels. Shelves lined with objects arranged in careful, almost tender symmetry: a wristwatch, a yellow barrette, a pair of prescription glasses repaired with blue tape.

Then he recognized the barrette.

The woman wearing it in the photograph behind the glass had been on a missing-person poster outside the supermarket. Her name was Elise something. Daniel remembered the picture because she was laughing, looking away from whoever held the camera.

In Martin’s photograph, she sat against a bare concrete wall.

She wasn’t laughing.

Daniel backed into the doorframe.

Along the opposite wall hung clothing sealed in clear garment bags. A waitress’s apron. A man’s checked shirt. A child-sized red raincoat that, when he looked closer, belonged to a very small woman. Dark stains had stiffened the fabric into folds. Below each bag, a card recorded a name, a date, and a place.

The smell reached him then, underneath the bleach: damp cloth, rust, something sweet gone rotten.

One cabinet held jewelry. Some pieces still carried traces of dried blood in their clasps. Another contained locks of hair tied with thread, each resting on a numbered square of white card.

Daniel stared at a silver ring with a pale groove worn around its inside edge. Someone had worn it every day. Someone had twisted it during meetings, taken it off beside a sink, searched for it in bedsheets.

He pressed both hands over his mouth.

There were photographs beneath the shelves, stacked in labeled envelopes. He saw enough of the top image to understand why Martin had needed a basement drain. He turned away before his mind could finish assembling it.

On the desk lay an open notebook.

The left page contained a list of names.

Most were crossed out.

On the right was a floor plan of Daniel’s house.

His bedroom was marked with an X.

Beside it, in Martin’s neat handwriting:

*No family nearby. Keeps back window open.*

Upstairs, a key entered a lock.

Daniel stopped breathing.

The front door opened. Grocery bags rustled. Martin spoke softly to the cat.

Then silence.

Daniel looked toward the stairs. The screwdriver was still in the broken basement latch.

“Daniel?” Martin called.

His voice held the same mild surprise it always did when they met at the mailbox.

Daniel pulled out his phone. His fingers slipped twice before he managed to dial.

Above him, a floorboard creaked.

“Oh,” Martin said.

The basement door closed.

The first warning was the silence: six hundred men in the dining hall, and suddenly no one lifting a fork.

Then a tray struck a guard across the face.

Noise rushed into the gap. Tables overturned. Men surged toward the doors, some attacking, others simply trying to get clear. A guard disappeared beneath a knot of gray uniforms; his baton rose once above the crowd, changed hands, and came down again.

“Lock it down!”

The order crackled from a radio already lying on the floor.

Steel shutters slammed over the serving windows. At the far exit, two officers braced behind a table while inmates hammered it forward, its legs shrieking against the concrete. Someone hurled a chair into the security camera. The image on the control-room monitor jerked sideways, leaving a tilted view of shoes, fallen trays, and one man crawling beneath a bench.

When the response team entered, their shields filled the doorway.

They advanced a few feet before the crowd hit them. Plastic shields buckled inward. Batons struck shoulders and forearms. An inmate grabbed a guard’s visor and pulled him down; another officer dragged his colleague free by the collar, stumbling backward while blows landed against his helmet.

Tear gas burst beside the overturned tables.

Now nobody could see much beyond the next body. Men coughed, swung blindly, collided. A prisoner who had been shouting seconds earlier crouched against the wall with his hands over his head. Nearby, an officer knelt beside someone who wasn’t moving, trying to protect them both with a shield too small for the job.

Above the din, the loudspeakers kept repeating the same instruction.

“Return to your cells.”

The doors to the cellblocks were locked.

The hotel had folded the towels into swans.

Mara moved hers off the desk before laying down a cloth. Across the room, Vincent sat beneath a painting of a sailboat, inspecting his pistol with the wounded concentration of a man checking a restaurant bill.

“Room service stops at eleven,” he said.

“It’s eleven-ten.”

“I know. That’s why I said it bitterly.”

Mara wiped a fingerprint from the handle of her knife. “There are almonds in the minibar.”

“Those are nine dollars.”

“You charged a man forty thousand dollars this morning.”

“And I intend to keep it.”

Rain tapped the window. Somewhere down the hall, a couple argued in the careful, muffled voices of people who believed a hotel door was soundproof.

Vincent glanced at the knife.

“Still your favorite?”

“No.”

“You carry it everywhere.”

“I carry reading glasses everywhere. They’re not my favorite way to kill someone either.”

“Could be. With ambition.”

She smiled despite herself.

He set his pistol on the cloth and leaned back. “All right. What is?”

“My favorite way?”

“Yes.”

“Canceled.”

“That’s not a way.”

“It is if the deposit clears.”

“You used to be more romantic about the profession.”

“I used to have cartilage.”

Vincent considered this. The ice machine groaned on the other side of the wall, followed by a thump like someone dropping a suitcase full of cutlery.

“I like distance,” he said.

“You like not having conversations.”

“Same thing.”

“You had a twenty-minute conversation with the concierge about olive oil.”

“The man was misinformed.”

Mara turned the knife in the lamplight, checking the blade. “Distance is impersonal.”

“It’s considerate. No introductions. No awkwardness.”

“No opportunity to discover you’ve got the wrong person.”

Vincent looked at her.

“That happened once,” he said.

“Twice.”

“The second man had his brother’s coat.”

“And face, apparently.”

He picked up the hotel stationery and wrote *ALMONDS — $9* at the top.

“What are you doing?”

“Expenses.”

“You haven’t eaten them.”

“I’m preparing emotionally.”

Mara put the knife away. For a while, the only sounds were the rain and Vincent’s pen scratching across the paper.

“I used to prefer getting close,” she said.

He stopped writing.

“Used to?”

“You could be sure. Look at someone and know.”

“Know what?”

“That they were the person in the photograph.”

“Ah.”

“What did you think I meant?”

“Something that would make this a much longer evening.”

She reached for the minibar and took out the almonds. The seal cracked sharply in the quiet.

Vincent watched her eat one.

“Those are my expenses.”

“Invoice me.”

He went back to his pistol. “Quiet. That’s my answer. Whatever leaves things quiet.”

“There’s always somebody making noise afterward.”

“I didn’t say it was a perfect system.”

The argument down the hall stopped. A door opened, then closed. A few seconds later, someone passed their room, crying softly.

Mara held the packet out to Vincent.

He took three almonds.

“These are stale.”

“They’re nine dollars. Try harder.”

He ate another.

On the desk, Mara’s phone lit up. She read the message without touching it.

“Well?” Vincent asked.

“Tomorrow’s canceled.”

“Deposit?”

“Cleared.”

He smiled and began putting his things away.

Mara reached for the room-service menu.

“It’s closed,” he reminded her.

“Breakfast.”

He held out his hand for it.

For the next ten minutes they discussed eggs, with considerably more conviction.

“My favorite way?”

“Yes.”

“Canceled.”

“That’s not a way.”

“It is if the deposit clears.”

“You used to be more romantic about the profession.”

“I used to have cartilage.”

Vincent considered this. The ice machine groaned on the other side of the wall, followed by a thump like someone dropping a suitcase full of cutlery.

“I like distance,” he said.

“You like not having conversations.”

“Same thing.”

“You had a twenty-minute conversation with the concierge about olive oil.”

“The man was misinformed.”

Mara turned the knife in the lamplight, checking the blade. “Distance is impersonal.”

“It’s considerate. No introductions. No awkwardness.”

“No opportunity to discover you’ve got the wrong person.”

Vincent looked at her.

“That happened once,” he said.

“Twice.”

“The second man had his brother’s coat.”

“And face, apparently.”

He picked up the hotel stationery and wrote ALMONDS — $9 at the top.

“What are you doing?”

“Expenses.”

“You haven’t eaten them.”

“I’m preparing emotionally.”

Mara put the knife away. For a while, the only sounds were the rain and Vincent’s pen scratching across the paper.

“I used to prefer getting close,” she said.

He stopped writing.

“Used to?”

“You could be sure. Look at someone and know.”

“Know what?”

“That they were the person in the photograph.”

“Ah.”

“What did you think I meant?”

“Something that would make this a much longer evening.”

She reached for the minibar and took out the almonds. The seal cracked sharply in the quiet.

Vincent watched her eat one.

“Those are my expenses.”

“Invoice me.”

He went back to his pistol. “Quiet. That’s my answer. Whatever leaves things quiet.”

“I didn’t say it was a perfect system.”

The argument down the hall stopped. A door opened, then closed. A few seconds later, someone passed their room, crying softly.

Mara held the packet out to Vincent.

He took three almonds.

“These are stale.”

“They’re nine dollars. Try harder.”

He ate another.

“Well?” Vincent asked.

“Tomorrow’s canceled.”

“Deposit?”

“Cleared.”

He smiled and began putting his things away.

Mara reached for the room-service menu.

“It’s closed,” he reminded her.

“Breakfast.”

He held out his hand for it.

For the next ten minutes they discussed eggs, with considerably more conviction.

The first grave opened like a mouth.

Earth split along the length of the mound, exhaling a cellar-stink of wet wool, spoiled meat, and rainwater trapped beneath stone. A hand emerged. The fingers were bare at their tips, yellow bone showing through scraps of blackened skin. They worried at the mud until the wrist came free.

On the hill above the burial field, the necromancer lifted his other hand.

A thousand graves answered.

They had buried the king’s army here after the winter siege, without coffins, without prayers, with their boots still on. Now the hillside stirred beneath its quilt of nettles. Rusted helmets surfaced. Elbows broke through turf. Men who had gone into the earth together dragged one another out.

Some retained their faces. Others wore loose masks of flesh, swollen by the thaw and slipping crookedly over their teeth. One soldier stood with his jaw hanging against his throat, working it patiently as if trying to remember how to speak. Another had roots threaded through his ribs. When he pulled himself upright, the young ash growing above him bent, shuddered, and came out of the ground.

The necromancer watched without triumph.

His name was Odran, though he had begun to forget what it sounded like in another person’s voice. Beneath his robe, the bells sewn into his skin rang softly.

There was no wind.

He opened the book.

Its pages were ordinary vellum. That was the worst of it. No screaming faces, no blood seeping from the binding: only neat brown handwriting and corrections made by a careful scholar. Beside the final invocation, someone had written *hold the breath through the third line*.

Odran obeyed.

The words left his mouth in the wrong order and arrived correctly somewhere below the world.

For a moment, the rain hung motionless. Each drop held a tiny image of the burial field—not as it was, but empty, every grave filled and undisturbed. Then the drops rose into the clouds.

Odran felt something take notice of him.

His shadow turned its head.

Downhill, the dead stopped climbing.

Every corpse looked toward him, including those whose eyes had rotted away. He could feel their attention pressing against his teeth. Beneath it lay another awareness, vast and incurious, testing the bodies as a hand might test the fit of gloves.

“Stand,” he whispered.

They stood.

A woman in a captain’s coat struggled with a leg that had come apart at the knee. She reached down, set the bones together, and waited. Darkness gathered inside the joint. It tightened with the small, domestic sound of thread being pulled through cloth.

Odran swallowed. The taste of grave soil filled his mouth.

He had expected resistance. He had prepared for rage, for pleading, for the dreadful recognition of men recalled from rest.

Instead, the captain saluted.

The others followed, thousands of ruined hands rising beneath the backward rain.

Then, somewhere in the ranks, a dead man began to cry.

Odran searched the faces but could not find him. The sound continued as he lowered his arm, as the army turned toward the distant lamps of the city.

When he gave the order to march, he made his voice loud enough to cover it.

The man in the chair kept saying he didn’t know them.

That was what Eli would remember afterward—not the warehouse or the cold, but how the man repeated it, patiently at first, as though someone had made a mistake that could still be corrected.

Rafe put a length of pipe into Eli’s hand.

“You wanted brothers,” he said. “Brothers don’t stand around when there’s work.”

The others closed the space behind him. Nobody shouted. One checked his phone. Another watched the door. Their boredom made it worse: this was ordinary to them.

“What did he do?” Eli asked.

Rafe’s expression hardened.

“You asking questions already?”

A few men laughed. Eli looked toward the exit, and someone stepped in front of it.

“Look at me,” Rafe said. “We fed you. Gave you somewhere to sleep. Told you things people don’t get to hear and walk away from.” He tapped the pipe with one finger. “Now we find out whether you meant what you said.”

The captive saw Eli hesitate.

“Please,” he whispered.

Eli struck him.

The chair toppled, and the man landed awkwardly, unable to put out his tied hands. He struggled to pull his knees toward his chest. Eli lowered the pipe, horrified by how quickly a standing, speaking person had become someone trying only to protect his head.

Rafe shook his head.

“Did I say you were finished?”

Eli’s grip loosened. Someone behind him pushed the pipe back against his palm.

The second blow brought a sound he had never heard from another person. The third came because Rafe was watching.

At last, Rafe caught his wrist.

“There,” he said warmly. “Wasn’t so hard.”

The others clapped Eli on the shoulders. One called him brother.

On the floor, the man was still moving. Eli started toward him, but Rafe steered him away.

“Leave him.”

Eli went with them. Behind him, he could hear the chair scraping as the man tried to get free.

By the time he asked whether I remembered the orchard, he had eaten half his supper.

“The pears,” he said. “Your father could never keep the wasps off them.”

I remembered my father standing on a ladder with his sleeves rolled up. I remembered this man arriving in a black motorcar, carrying papers my father could not read.

“He tried hanging jars in the branches,” I said.

“Did he?”

“You told him to.”

He smiled as though I had returned something he had misplaced.

Between us, the candles burned steadily. I had expected some disturbance in the room—a draft, a guttering flame—but the house continued its ordinary noises. The clock struck the quarter. Beyond the door, a servant set down a tray.

He took another mouthful.

For three years I had imagined watching closely. I had believed there would be a particular instant when I could say: there. Now.

Instead, he talked about the roads.

“The bridge will need replacing before winter. I’ve told the council twice.”

His knife stopped moving.

He looked down at his hand, mildly annoyed, then adjusted his grip.

“Twice,” he repeated.

“Perhaps they’ll listen this time.”

He reached for his wine. The rim clicked against his teeth.

I watched a little wine escape down his chin. He caught it with his napkin and examined the red mark.

“Clumsy of me.”

“You’ve had a long day.”

“Yes.”

He shifted in his chair. A sheen had appeared along his upper lip, though the dining room was cool enough that I had kept my shawl. He tugged at his collar and asked whether the fire was necessary.

“It’s nearly out,” I said.

“Nevertheless.”

I could have rung for someone to remove the log. My hand stayed beside my plate.

He tried to resume his story about the bridge, but halfway through a sentence he seemed to lose interest in it. His eyes moved toward the window. Then to the door.

“Something disagrees with me.”

The words were ordinary. He might have said them on any evening.

I had expected satisfaction to arrive with them. Instead, I noticed that a button on his waistcoat was hanging by a thread. Someone would have been told to mend it tomorrow.

He pressed his palm against his stomach.

“Ring for Mrs. Vale.”

I looked at the bellpull beside the hearth.

“Please,” he added.

That was worse. I had prepared myself for anger, for suspicion, even for his hand closing around my wrist. I had not prepared for manners.

His breathing grew quicker. He sat forward, then leaned back abruptly, unable to find a position that eased him. When he reached for the water, his fingers knocked the glass over. It rolled once across the cloth and stopped against the salt cellar.

We both watched the water spread.

“What have you—”

He stopped. Whether he could not finish or would not, I never knew.

I stood, and his eyes followed me to the hearth.

My father had begged this man for one more month. I had been outside the study, holding his wet coat. All these years, that was where I had remained: outside a closed door, listening.

Now there was no door between us.

I caught the bellpull and rang until I heard running in the passage.

Then I went back to the table. He was still looking at me, waiting for an answer, and for the first time that evening I could not meet his eyes.

results.model_response:
The plank dipped beneath Caleb’s bare foot.

Behind him, the crew stood silent along the rail. Men who had drunk beside him, cursed beside him, whispered their promises in the dark. Now none would meet his eyes.

Captain Vane rested one hand on the pommel of his sword.

“You wanted the ship,” he said. “There she is. Take a good look.”

Caleb turned. The *Mercy* rose above him, black hull streaked with salt, her sails swollen against a white sky. From here she looked impossibly solid. A world with floors and walls and somewhere to sleep.

The plank creaked.

“Captain.” His voice came out thin. He swallowed and tried again. “I have money in Nassau.”

“So you mentioned.”

“More than I told you.”

Vane said nothing.

Below, something long and gray slipped beneath the surface.

Caleb stopped breathing.

He had known about the sharks. The whole crew had watched them following the galley refuse that morning. Knowing was different from seeing one turn beneath his feet, its shadow bending slowly through the green water.

“Please.”

The word seemed to embarrass the men more than the mutiny had.

Vane drew his sword and laid its point against Caleb’s back.

Caleb shuffled forward. A splinter caught under his heel; absurdly, he wanted to sit down and pull it out. He thought of his boots beside his hammock. He had left a good pair of boots.

At the end of the plank, there was nowhere else to put his foot.

“No,” he whispered.

The captain pressed.

Caleb fell with both arms reaching backward.

The sea closed over his head. For a moment the ship vanished, the shouting vanished, and there was only cold water and the furious thud of his heart.

He surfaced coughing.

“Rope!” he screamed. “Throw me a rope!”

Someone moved at the rail.

“Stand fast,” said Vane.

Caleb struck out toward the hull. He could see the weed growing along its seams. He reached for it, his fingertips scraping wet timber.

A fin broke the surface behind him.

The first strike pulled him sideways. His cry brought a young deckhand stumbling away from the rail. Water churned white against the hull, then darkened red. Caleb surfaced once more, grasping at empty air, before another rush from below took him under.

The crew waited for him to come back.

His hand appeared briefly beyond the foam.

Then it was gone.

Vane sheathed his sword.

“Bring in the plank.”

Two sailors obeyed. Neither spoke. As they hauled the wet timber aboard, a single drop fell from its end onto the deck.

The youngest deckhand stared at it until the boatswain ordered him back to work.

At the end of the plank, there was nowhere else to put his foot.

“No,” he whispered.

The captain pressed.

Caleb fell with both arms reaching backward.

The sea closed over his head. For a moment the ship vanished, the shouting vanished, and there was only cold water and the furious thud of his heart.

He surfaced coughing.

“Rope!” he screamed. “Throw me a rope!”

Someone moved at the rail.

“Stand fast,” said Vane.

Caleb struck out toward the hull. He could see the weed growing along its seams. He reached for it, his fingertips scraping wet timber.

A fin broke the surface behind him.

The first strike pulled him sideways. His cry brought a young deckhand stumbling away from the rail. Water churned white against the hull, then darkened red. Caleb surfaced once more, grasping at empty air, before another rush from below took him under.

The crew waited for him to come back.

His hand appeared briefly beyond the foam.

Then it was gone.

Vane sheathed his sword.

“Bring in the plank.”

Two sailors obeyed. Neither spoke. As they hauled the wet timber aboard, a single drop fell from its end onto the deck.

The youngest deckhand stared at it until the boatswain ordered him back to work.

The first night, the knocking came from the cellar.

Three soft taps. A pause. Three more.

Elias sat upright in bed and listened until dawn, holding his breath whenever the house creaked. In the morning, he went downstairs and stood over the fresh cement.

A pipe, he decided. An old house settling.

He did not look at the hammer.

By the fourth night, the knocking had moved inside the walls.

It followed him from room to room, always at the height of a person’s hand. When he climbed the stairs, it climbed beside him. When he stopped, it stopped.

“Enough,” he whispered.

A woman on the other side of the plaster whispered it back.

He slept in the kitchen with every light burning. At some point before morning, exhaustion lowered his head onto his folded arms.

He dreamed of the last thing Mara had said.

Not a curse. Not even a plea.

*Elias?*

His name, spoken with such bewilderment that he had struck her again to stop hearing it.

He woke to find two cups on the table.

One held cold coffee. The other was full of wet earth.

After that, he stopped trusting the house.

The mirror above the bathroom sink showed the doorway behind him, and sometimes Mara stood there in her blue coat. If he turned, she vanished. If he kept watching, she remained perfectly still until his eyes watered.

Once, he made himself hold her gaze.

Her reflection lifted one hand to the back of her head.

Elias tore the mirror off its hooks and carried it outside. He left it facedown in the rain, then returned to the bathroom and washed his hands. In the dark window above the sink, she was closer.

He began drinking from the tap. He could not bear cups anymore.

Food became impossible. Bread left grit between his teeth. An apple split under his knife and exposed a small white tooth where the seeds should have been. He dropped it, stepped back, and saw only an apple on the floor.

He left it there.

His sister called. He let the telephone ring until it stopped.

Then it rang again.

“I know it’s you,” he said when he answered.

“Elias?” his sister asked.

He threw the telephone against the wall.

For an hour afterward, from among the broken pieces, Mara kept saying his name.

On the ninth day, he went to the cellar with a shovel.

He had decided to confess. He would uncover her, call the police, and wait outside. He practiced the words as he struck the cement.

*I killed my wife.*

The shovel skidded. Sparks flashed in the dimness.

*I killed Mara.*

Behind him, a stair creaked.

He did not turn.

“I’m going to tell them.”

Another creak, lower down.

“I’ll tell them everything.”

He worked until his palms opened. When the shovel became too painful to hold, he knelt and pulled at the broken cement with his fingers.

Underneath was dirt.

He dug deeper.

Dirt filled his cuffs. It packed beneath his nails. He found the corner of the sheet and recoiled so violently that he struck his head against the wall.

For a long time he crouched there, watching it.

The sheet moved.

Only slightly—a small tightening, as though someone beneath it had drawn one knee toward her chest.

“No,” he said.

He had checked. That night, he had checked and checked.

The cellar light went out.

In the darkness, he heard fabric dragging over earth.

He crawled toward the stairs. His hands found the bottom step, but when he raised his head, the staircase seemed to continue upward farther than the house could possibly allow. At the distant top stood Mara.

Behind him, something sat up.

He squeezed his eyes shut.

He tried to remember his sister’s number. He tried to remember whether it was morning. He tried, desperately, to remember Mara before the cellar: asleep beside him, impatient in a queue, laughing with her mouth full.

But every memory ended with her turning toward him.

Every time, she saw what he was holding.

A hand settled on his shoulder.

Elias began to apologize. He spoke quickly at first, then carefully, searching for words she might accept.

Long after his voice failed, his mouth kept moving.

The city had finally gotten him alone.

It did that sooner or later. Took you down an alley, whispered something sweet through a mouthful of rotten teeth, and emptied your pockets while you were still trying to understand the joke.

He lay beside the dumpster with his coat spread beneath him, almost considerate. The rain had darkened everything it touched. There was blood where the rain couldn’t reach, and enough of it to make the uniform behind me find something else to look at.

I kept looking. That was the job.

Above us, an elevated train rattled past. For six seconds it drowned out the rain, the traffic, the kid behind me being sick. Then it was gone, carrying warm people toward apartments where somebody had left a light on.

The dead man wore good shoes. Hand-stitched, recently polished. One heel had come loose in the struggle. His left hand still held a scrap of somebody else’s sleeve.

I crouched without touching him.

People called this town a machine. They gave it too much credit. Machines could be repaired. This place was an old wound under a clean shirt, and every election they changed the shirt.

“Robbery?” the uniform asked.

The victim’s watch caught the light from my flashlight. Gold. Probably real.

“Not a successful one.”

I looked at the scrap in his fist again. Cheap gray cloth, torn along a seam.

For once, the city had left me something besides a body and the bill.

By midnight, the city had stopped pretending not to watch.

Every apartment window along the avenue glowed blue with the broadcast. Mara could see herself on the screens as she ran beneath them: a small white figure stumbling through rain, an arrow hovering above her head.

**RUNNER 06.**

The number had replaced her name at sentencing.

She turned into a pharmacy and slipped on broken glass. Pain flared in her ankle. Behind the empty prescription counter, an advertisement still promised relief in twelve minutes or less.

The announcer’s voice followed her through the ceiling speakers.

“An unexpected detour. She’s conserving distance, but has she sacrificed visibility?”

Mara pressed both hands over her mouth.

Outside, boots entered the puddles one deliberate step at a time.

She had seen the hunter before the gates opened: silver coat, expensive teeth, a rifle held loosely while an attendant adjusted its sling. He had shaken hands with the other contestants. Someone had brought him coffee.

Now his shadow crossed the pharmacy doorway.

Mara crawled toward the rear exit. Above its handle, a municipal lock blinked amber.

She pushed it.

**ACCESS RESTRICTED DURING LIVE EVENTS.**

She pushed again.

“Please,” she whispered.

The lock repeated its message at a higher volume.

The hunter found her there.

For a moment neither moved. His coat shed rain onto the tiles. A little camera floated over his shoulder, correcting its angle until both their faces were visible.

“Hands where I can see them.”

Mara raised them.

“I have a daughter.”

He glanced at the camera. It had drifted close enough for her to see its lens opening.

“On your knees.”

“The intake form has her old address. If they send the notice there, she won’t know.”

His expression changed—not enough to help her, but enough that she saw he had understood.

Mara lowered herself carefully. Her injured ankle would not bend. She had to sit crookedly against the door.

The hunter touched his earpiece.

“Six secured.”

A pause.

“No. Alive.”

The camera’s green light went red.

He waited, listening. Mara watched a drop of water gather at his cuff and fall between them.

“I know what the bonus is,” he said.

Two retrieval officers arrived carrying a restraint frame. One checked the number on Mara’s collar while the other fitted the cuffs.

“Where are you taking me?” she asked.

Neither answered. They lifted her before she could get her good foot underneath her.

“My daughter’s name is Esme,” she told the hunter. “Esme Vale. South district.”

He stepped aside to let the frame pass.

At the doorway, Mara twisted toward him.

“Will you remember?”

The announcer returned before he answered.

“A clean capture! Excellent discipline from tonight’s defending champion.”

Outside, a platform unfolded from the side of a broadcast van. An attendant hurried forward with a towel and a velvet case. The hunter dried his hands. Behind him, the retrieval officers loaded Mara into an unmarked vehicle.

The attendant opened the case. Inside lay a gold pin shaped like a running figure.

“Your sixth,” she said.

He held still while she fastened it to his lapel.

On the monitor beside the camera, his prize balance increased. Beneath it appeared the customary question.

**DONATE A PORTION TO DEPENDENTS OF THE CONDEMNED?**

He selected yes.

The audience rating rose three points.

results.model_response:
The shovel had been made for earth.

Private Ellis thought of that afterward. Beforeward, it was simply a weight against his hip, its shortened handle polished by wet gloves and the heel of his hand. He had used it that afternoon to scrape a sleeping shelf into the trench wall. There was still a thread of pale root caught beneath the blade.

The bombardment stopped at four minutes past dawn.

Ellis knew the time because Sergeant Bell had made him check his watch. He did not know why that mattered now, with the firing step broken and Bell somewhere beneath it.

In the silence after the shells, dirt continued to fall.

Then a man dropped into the trench.

He landed badly, one knee striking the duckboards. His rifle hit the wall. For an instant he and Ellis stared at each other across the narrow passage, both bent forward, both breathing through open mouths.

Ellis saw the unfamiliar helmet first. Then the bayonet.

The man pulled his rifle free.

Ellis tried to bring up his own, but its sling had caught beneath a timber. He hauled at it once. The other soldier thrust, and the bayonet went through the loose cloth beneath Ellis’s arm and struck the trench wall.

They collided.

There was no room for the movements they had practiced behind the lines. Ellis could not get his feet beneath him. His shoulder scraped a nail. The German shoved him backward, trying to draw the bayonet out, and Ellis caught the rifle barrel with both hands.

For several seconds they wrestled over it.

The German smelled of damp wool. His face was inches away, young and unshaven, with mud dried in the creases beside his nose. He made a strained, impatient sound as he pulled. Ellis’s grip slipped along the barrel.

The shovel handle pressed against his hip.

He let go with one hand.

The first blow struck the helmet and jarred his arm to the elbow. The German ducked, driving forward. Ellis hit the wall hard enough to lose his breath. He swung again, awkwardly, with hardly any space, and the edge struck the man’s cheek.

The German cried out. Blood ran over Ellis’s knuckles.

Still he fought.

That was what Ellis had not understood before: a man could be badly hurt and remain strong. The rifle fell between them, but the German seized Ellis by the throat and forced him down onto one knee. Ellis could hear a thin whistling noise and realized it came from himself.

He struck with the shovel again.

The grip loosened.

He struck once more, using both hands now.

The German fell sideways against the duckboards. His boots knocked against the rifle. He tried to lift his head, and Ellis, terrified that he would stand, brought the blade down again.

Afterward, there was only Ellis’s breathing.

He remained crouched with the shovel raised. His arms trembled so violently that he could not lower it without knocking the blade against the wall.

Someone was firing farther along the trench. A voice shouted for bombs.

The German lay at his feet, one hand open beside his face. Ellis watched that hand. He expected it to close.

“Stay down,” he said.

The man did not move.

Ellis swallowed. His throat hurt where the fingers had pressed it.

“Stay down.”

He heard himself and stopped.

He had never been so glad of anything as he was that the man was dead. The relief came first, warm and enormous. He was alive. He could breathe. The bayonet had missed him.

Then he looked at the shovel.

He dropped it so abruptly that the handle struck his shin.

Corporal Vane appeared around the traverse, carrying a sack of grenades.

“You hit?”

Ellis shook his head.

Vane looked at the body and then at the torn sleeve.

“Get your rifle. They’re in the next bay.”

Ellis bent to lift it. His hands would not work properly. He could see what they needed to do, but his fingers kept slipping from the sling. There was blood beneath his nails. He rubbed them against his trousers, then rubbed them again.

Vane caught his shoulder.

“Ellis. Your rifle.”

“Yes.”

He freed it from beneath the timber.

As he straightened, his boot touched the German’s open hand. Ellis stepped back at once.

“Sorry,” he said.

Vane had already turned away.

Ellis stood alone for another moment, staring at the man he had killed. He tried to remember the face as it had looked when they first saw each other. It had been intact then. There had been an expression on it.

He could not recover it.

From the next bay came a shout, followed by a blast that shook loose more earth. Ellis flinched and raised his rifle. He went toward Vane, leaving the shovel where it lay.

By law, the square had to be full.

Each apartment block supplied twenty spectators. Each school sent a class. The bakeries closed for an hour, though their ovens stayed lit, and the smell of warm bread drifted between the government banners.

**SMALL CRIMES MAKE BROKEN NATIONS**, the banners said.

At eleven, the officials brought out the boy.

He was sixteen, according to the notice nailed beside the platform. His name was Tomas Vale. His crime was the theft of one plain loaf, weighing seven hundred grams, from a licensed provisioner.

Someone in the crowd whispered, “Seven hundred.”

“Quiet,” said someone else.

The boy’s coat was too short at the wrists. That was what Mara noticed. She had prepared herself for everything else—the guards, the sentence, the apparatus behind the black screen—but not for those pale wrists protruding from a coat he had outgrown.

Beside her stood her daughter’s class, arranged in pairs. Their teacher walked along the line, reminding them to keep their hands out of their pockets.

The magistrate began his address.

He spoke about supply chains. About civic trust. About the damage caused when citizens confused personal need with public entitlement.

Near the fountain, a man called, “Thieves know the law.”

People turned toward him with visible relief. Several nodded. Agreement gave them something to do with their faces.

The licensed baker stood beneath the platform, holding his cap in both hands. He had reported the theft because failure to report was itself an offense. Now an official leaned down and asked him to confirm the value of the stolen goods.

The baker opened his mouth.

“Three credits,” the official prompted.

“Yes,” said the baker.

“Clearly, please.”

“Three credits.”

On the platform, Tomas looked over the crowd. A woman near Mara raised her hand a little, then lowered it before he could see.

The magistrate finished speaking.

The teacher faced the children. “Eyes forward.”

Behind the screen, a guard gave a short instruction. Mara heard the boy ask something, but the words did not carry.

Then came a heavy mechanical sound.

The pigeons lifted from the courthouse roof.

For a moment, the square was quiet enough to hear their wings.

The man by the fountain began clapping. He stopped after three claps, looked toward the officials, and started again. Others joined him. A government clerk moved slowly along the edge of the crowd, watching.

Mara brought her hands together.

Her daughter was staring up at her.

She kept clapping.

The baker had bent to pick up his cap, although he had not dropped it. He remained bent until an official touched his shoulder.

When the applause was over, the children were instructed to recite the civic pledge. Some spoke too quickly and had to wait for the others. One little boy had forgotten the words; his partner whispered them to him, a phrase at a time.

The gates opened at eleven fifteen.

People hurried out, anxious now about work, about the trams, about being marked late after an authorized absence. The woman who had raised her hand stayed where she was until the square wardens approached her.

On the walk home, Mara’s daughter asked whether the boy had eaten any of the bread.

Mara looked behind them.

“I don’t know,” she said.

At the bakery, they joined the queue.

The smell reached her before she opened the bathroom door. It had seeped into the hallway: a thick, spoiled sweetness layered over sewage and the sulfurous stink of rotten eggs. Underneath was something sharper, like ammonia, that caught in her nose and made her eyes water. She stopped with her hand on the knob. For a moment she tried to identify some ordinary cause—a blocked drain, food left to rot—but she already knew neither would account for it.

The bathroom was warm. A week with the window shut had left condensation on the mirror and a damp film on the tiles. In the tub, the body lay partly submerged in cloudy water. It was swollen enough to look unfamiliar, its contours rounded and distorted. The skin had darkened unevenly, greenish across the abdomen, purple-gray elsewhere, with branching stains beneath the surface. The hands resting near the waterline were pale and deeply wrinkled. She could not make herself look at the face for more than a second.

She took one involuntary breath through her mouth and gagged. That was worse: now the odor seemed to coat her tongue. She backed into the hallway, pressing her sleeve against her nose, but the fabric did almost nothing. A fly ticked against the frosted window behind her. She heard it stop, then start again.

Even after she reached the open front door, the clean air did not feel clean. She could still smell the bathroom on her sleeve, in her hair—or thought she could—and every attempt at a deeper breath brought another wave of nausea.

The collector shut the garage door before he took the bat out of its canvas sleeve.

Eddie stood beside the workbench with his hands open.

“I get paid Friday.”

“You said that last Friday.”

Somewhere behind the wall, a washing machine thumped through an uneven spin cycle. The collector glanced toward it, then back at Eddie.

“Sit down.”

Eddie shook his head. When the collector stepped closer, he tried to get around the workbench. A jar of screws went over, scattering across the concrete.

The first swing knocked him down.

His shout filled the low garage. He grabbed for the workbench, caught the edge of a drawer, and pulled it out on top of himself. He hardly seemed to notice.

“Wait.” The word came out breathless. “Wait, I’ve got some of it.”

The collector moved around him. Eddie dragged himself backward on his elbows until his shoulders hit the closed door.

Afterward, there was only the washing machine and Eddie trying to breathe.

Both legs lay still. When he tried to move one, pain stopped him. He stared down, then up at the collector, his mouth working before any words came.

“Call somebody.”

The collector put the bat back in its sleeve. His cuff had ridden up; he straightened it with two fingers.

“Friday,” he said.

Eddie had begun to shake. He pressed his palms flat against the concrete as though he could steady himself that way.

“My phone’s on the bench.”

The collector looked at it. For a moment Eddie thought he would leave it there.

Instead, he set it on the floor within reach, lifted the garage door, and stepped into the daylight.

Eddie fumbled the phone twice before he could make the call.

The forest went quiet by degrees.

First the wind dropped. Then the small, busy sounds in the undergrowth stopped. At last there was only the woman ahead of him, moving through the dark with one hand held out against the branches.

He could hear the keys in her other hand.

Every few steps they chimed together—a bright domestic sound, absurd among the trees. He pictured the door they belonged to. A porch light. Mail left on a table. Somewhere, a room was waiting for her to return and become ordinary again.

She stopped.

He stopped too.

“Hello?”

He liked this part least: the invitation to become a person.

If he answered, he would need a voice, an excuse, perhaps even a name. There would be rules again. People expected things from a man who spoke.

So he let the forest answer. A branch creaked overhead.

She turned and continued, faster now.

For years he had told himself that he enjoyed the silence. It was a pleasing explanation, almost harmless. Other men went fishing. Other men sat in parked cars long after arriving home.

But there was no silence inside him now. He felt intensely awake. The cold touched every finger separately. He noticed the pale undersides of leaves, the smell of wet bark, a loose thread brushing his wrist.

During the day, hours disappeared without his noticing. He answered questions at work and forgot what he had said. He ate standing at the kitchen counter. Here, he could remember every moment afterward.

Ahead, she stumbled. The keys rang out.

He smiled before he could help it.

*There you are.*

Not the woman from the roadside, irritated by a wrong turn, lifting her phone toward a sky it could not reach. That woman had seemed barely aware of the woods.

Now she listened to them.

To him.

That was what he had never admitted, even privately: he wanted to occupy another person’s mind completely. He wanted every thought she had to concern where he was.

She reached a fallen tree and went around it. Beyond her, between the trunks, a faint yellow light appeared.

He had forgotten the houses on the far side of the forest.

The sight irritated him. He wanted more time.

She saw it too.

“Help!”

The word came out hoarse, much louder than her earlier call. She ran toward the light, breaking branches, no longer trying to be quiet.

He followed, and for a few seconds the woods became confused with noise. His coat caught on something. He pulled free too sharply and struck his shoulder against a trunk.

Then he heard another voice.

“Who’s there?”

A man, some distance away. A door banged.

He stopped.

Through the trees he glimpsed the woman crossing a patch of illuminated ground. Someone reached toward her. She caught that person’s arm with both hands.

He waited for her to look back.

She didn’t.

The door closed, leaving a yellow rectangle across the empty yard.

He stood in the dark with his shoulder aching. His breath sounded unpleasantly loud. Gradually the woods resumed around him: water dripping, leaves shifting, something small moving beneath the fallen tree.

He put a hand against the place where his coat had torn.

He had liked to think that he came here because, here, he felt nothing.

Now he could not make himself leave the light.

I woke with my cheek against cold stone and the taste of metal in my mouth.

For a moment, I thought the darkness was something wrong with my eyes. Then a lamp guttered somewhere above me, and the room appeared in pieces: a low ceiling, sweating walls, a drain beneath a wooden chair.

The smell came next. Old blood, heavy and stale beneath the sharper tang of rust. Damp leather. Sour water. I tried breathing through my mouth, but the air seemed to coat my tongue.

I lifted my head. A chain scraped across the floor.

There were implements hanging on the opposite wall, arranged with an orderliness that made me colder than the stone had. Pliers in several sizes. Hooks. A narrow saw with a dark wooden handle. Some objects I couldn’t identify, though I found myself studying them, trying to decide which edges were meant to cut and which parts were meant to close.

Below them stood a table. Its surface had been scrubbed pale in places, but the seams between the boards were black. A folded cloth lay beside a basin, neatly squared at the corners.

I looked away.

The chair near the drain had straps at the arms and ankles. One hung loose, its buckle almost touching the floor. There was an ordinary stool beside it, positioned where someone could sit comfortably and work.

Beyond the lamp’s reach, water dripped at uneven intervals. I listened for footsteps between the drops.

When I tried to stand, the chain pulled tight. I sat down slowly, keeping it as quiet as I could.

Only then did I notice the door. Light showed beneath it, and for a while I watched that thin strip, afraid of the moment a shadow would cross it.

The vault timer read **04:59** when the first siren sounded.

“That’s not possible,” Voss said.

Mara stood behind the counter with a canvas bag in one hand and her pistol pointed at the marble floor. Through the bank’s tall windows, blue lights slid across the wet street.

“You said three minutes,” she told him.

“I said the alarm was cut.”

On the floor, the branch manager closed her eyes.

The timer changed to **04:58**.

Then Danny fired at the security camera.

The shot struck like a hammer inside a steel drum. Glass sprinkled from the black dome in the ceiling. Customers screamed and pressed themselves flatter against the floor. Mara ducked before she could stop herself.

“What the hell are you doing?”

Danny stared up at the broken camera, both hands locked around his gun. He was twenty-two and had been smiling in the car.

He wasn’t smiling now.

Outside, a patrol car stopped broadside across the entrance. An officer crouched behind its door.

“Put down your weapons! Come out with your hands visible!”

Voss seized the manager by her collar.

“Back exit.”

“It opens into a service court.”

“Show me.”

Mara looked toward the street. Across the road, their getaway driver stepped out of the sedan with his palms raised.

Voss saw him too.

For a second, nobody moved.

Then Danny shouted, “He’s giving us up,” and fired through the window.

The pane whitened around the bullet hole before collapsing in a glittering sheet. An officer beside the second cruiser fell against its hood and disappeared behind it.

The answer came almost immediately.

Shots snapped through the bank. The brass rail beside Mara rang like a struck bell. Plaster burst over the teller stations, filling the air with pale dust. She dropped behind the counter as fragments pattered across her coat.

Danny staggered backward.

He looked puzzled. His pistol slipped from his fingers, hit the floor, and skidded beneath a chair. He sat down heavily beside the deposit-slip stand. Blood spread across the front of his gray sweatshirt.

“Mara?”

She crawled toward him.

Another volley struck the counter. She flattened herself, cheek against cold marble, and watched a pen roll slowly past her nose.

“Stay down!” someone outside shouted. “Everybody stay down!”

Voss fired from beside a pillar. Each muzzle flash lit his face in a hard orange blink. Mara had known that face for six years. Now she could barely recognize it.

Near the entrance, a uniformed bank guard lay motionless beside an overturned chair. His glasses had landed several feet away, one lens still intact.

The manager was trying to crawl toward a woman who had been struck in the shoulder. The woman held her arm tightly against herself. Blood ran between her fingers and stained the sleeve of her cream coat.

“Help her,” Mara said.

The manager stared at the gun in Mara’s hand.

Mara set it on the floor and pushed it away.

“Please.”

Voss turned.

“Pick that up.”

“No.”

From outside came another burst of shots. Voss jerked against the pillar and slid down it, leaving a dark smear on the pale stone. His weapon clattered beside him.

The silence afterward was incomplete: sirens, sobbing, broken glass settling somewhere overhead.

Mara reached Danny. His breaths were quick and shallow.

“Did we get it?” he whispered.

She glanced toward the vault.

**03:12.**

“No.”

He swallowed. His eyes drifted toward the ceiling.

She pressed both hands against the wound in his chest and called for help until her voice failed.

When the police entered, Mara was still kneeling beside him. She obeyed when they told her to move away. An officer pulled her hands behind her back while another crouched over Danny.

Through the shattered windows, she could see paramedics working beside the cruiser. One officer held a blood-soaked dressing against his partner’s side, speaking to him with urgent, steady patience.

The vault clicked open while they were leading her out.

Nobody turned to look.

The first sign was the taste.

Bitter metal at the back of her tongue. Mara swallowed, rubbed her mouth with her sleeve, and looked toward the vent above the door.

Something hissed behind the grille.

She tried the handle. Locked.

“No.” She tried again, harder, lifting as she turned it. The latch rattled without moving. “Hey! There’s someone in here!”

Her voice came back small and flat.

She struck the door with the heel of her hand. Then both fists. At first she paused between blows to listen. Soon she stopped listening.

The air looked exactly the same. That was the worst part: the ordinary light, the empty chair, her jacket hanging from its hook. Nothing she could point to or push away.

Her eyes began to water. She blinked hard, but the door blurred anyway.

She pulled her collar over her nose and searched the room. Vent. Chair. Hinges. There had to be something. She dragged the chair beneath the grille, its legs shrieking across the floor, and climbed onto it.

The first cough folded her over.

She clutched the chair back until it passed, then reached up. Her fingers scraped the screws. She had no tool. She tried turning one with her thumbnail, pressing until the nail bent painfully.

Another cough. Her foot slipped.

She landed badly, one knee striking the floor. For several seconds she could only sit there, shocked by how much effort it took to draw breath. Her chest felt tight. A dull pressure swelled behind her forehead.

Get up.

She crawled to the door instead.

“Please.” She put her mouth near the gap. “Please, open it.”

She waited for footsteps. Heard a rushing sound and thought, for one bright instant, that someone was coming.

But the sound stayed with her when she turned her head.

Her hands had begun to tremble. She reached for the handle and missed it, then stared at her fingers as though they belonged to someone else. What had she been trying to do?

The lock. Of course. The lock.

She pulled herself halfway upright. Her knees gave way before she reached it.

Her shoulder struck the door, and she slid down against it. She wanted to knock again, to make one last loud noise. Her hand lifted a few inches from the floor.

Then it settled back.

The handle remained above her, bright and impossibly far away.

By the time Officer Vale reached the apartment, he had stopped thinking of the dead man by his name.

Names created obligations. The body in the service alley was a problem of chronology.

At 11:42, a camera had recorded Vale’s cruiser turning off Mercer. At 11:51, a woman in the building across the street had heard a shot. Between those two facts lay nine minutes he would have to explain.

Unless someone else had to explain them first.

The young man in the apartment doorway wore supermarket trousers and one sock. Behind him, a television played to an empty sofa.

“Daniel Reyes?” Vale asked.

“Yes.”

“Mind if I come in?”

“What’s this about?”

Vale let a little silence pass. People often filled silence by surrendering something.

Reyes stepped aside.

The apartment was smaller than Vale expected. A drying rack occupied half the kitchen. There were envelopes arranged beside a calculator, a bowl holding three oranges, a child’s drawing fixed to the refrigerator.

“Anyone else here?”

“My daughter’s at her mother’s.”

Vale glanced at the drawing again. Two figures beneath a yellow sun. He had a daughter, too, though she no longer drew pictures for him.

That was irrelevant.

“Where were you tonight?”

“Working. Until ten. Then here.”

“Alone?”

“Yes.”

Reyes watched him now with the strained attention of someone trying to discover what answer had been wrong.

Vale had seen the expression hundreds of times. He had once interpreted it as guilt. Experience had taught him it was merely fear, which was more useful. Fear supplied hesitation, confusion, contradictory details. Later, all of those could be described without mentioning their cause.

There was still time to leave.

The thought arrived without urgency. He considered it as he might consider taking another street around roadworks.

He could walk out, return to the station, ask for a lawyer. There would be consequences, but they would at least belong to him.

Then he pictured Lieutenant Shaw looking through the glass of an interview room.

No.

“Wait by the door,” he told Reyes.

“Do you have a warrant?”

Vale turned.

The question had been timid, almost apologetic. He disliked it anyway.

“We’re trying to clear something up,” he said. “Don’t make it harder.”

Reyes looked toward the hallway, where Vale’s partner was speaking into her radio. Vale had deliberately left her with the neighbors. She was diligent. She would produce a clean account of everything she had actually witnessed.

When Reyes moved, Vale slipped the dead man’s watch beneath a cushion.

The act took less time than the decision had.

He stood with his hand still resting on the sofa. For a moment, the room looked exactly as it had before. The laundry, the calculator, the oranges. Nothing announced that its occupant’s life had changed.

Reyes said, “Am I supposed to call somebody?”

Vale did not answer. He called his partner instead.

“Mara. In here.”

She appeared at the door with her notebook open.

“What have you got?”

“Possible property from the victim.”

He disliked the word *possible*, but it belonged in the sentence. Certainty too early looked like foreknowledge.

Mara approached the sofa. Reyes took a step forward.

“What property?”

“Stay there,” she said.

Vale watched her find the watch. Watched recognition pass over her face. Now there was another witness to the evidence, and her surprise was genuine.

“That’s not mine,” Reyes said.

Vale had expected those words. He had expected them so precisely that hearing them brought relief.

Mara asked Reyes to put his hands behind his back.

“No. Listen. I’ve never seen that.”

Vale began arranging the report in his head. The lawful-sounding verbs. The sequence of observations. He would have to include Reyes’s denial; leaving it out would look worse. He would quote it accurately.

As Mara fastened the cuffs, Reyes looked directly at him.

“You know,” he said.

It was not loud. That made it harder to dismiss.

Vale met his eyes. He calculated whether to appear offended or confused and chose neither.

“You’ll have a chance to explain,” he said.

Then he stepped aside so Mara could lead him out.

The cache was six tins beneath the floor of an abandoned pharmacy. Two had split their seams. Three bulged at the lids. The last had no label.

Mara set them on the counter, beside a cash register full of worthless bills.

“Don’t open the swollen ones,” she said.

Across from her, the old man stared at the tins. His hands shook against the length of pipe he carried.

Behind him stood a woman in a yellow raincoat and a boy whose cheeks had hollowed around his teeth. Mara’s brother, Eli, blocked the doorway with a chair leg clenched in both hands.

There had been fourteen of them in the shelter that morning. These five were the only ones still strong enough to search.

The boy reached first.

Eli caught his wrist. The woman lunged at Eli with a screwdriver, and suddenly everyone was moving.

Mara heard the pipe hit her brother’s shoulder—a flat, ugly sound—and watched his arm drop. He struck back with the chair leg in his other hand. It glanced off the old man’s temple, sending him against a shelf of empty medicine bottles.

“Stop,” Mara shouted.

Nobody seemed to hear her.

The boy scrambled onto the counter and gathered tins against his chest. Mara grabbed his coat. He twisted away, pulling her off balance, and they fell together into the broken glass behind the register.

Pain flashed through her palm. She let go.

Eli had the woman pinned against the doorframe. She drove a knee into his stomach, then stabbed at him again. The screwdriver caught his thigh. He sagged, trying to hold himself upright with his useless arm.

The old man came toward the counter with his pipe raised.

Mara found a shard of shelving beside her—a strip of metal with one end bent into a hook. She swung it at his knees.

He fell hard. His pipe clattered away, and for a moment his cries were the only sound in the pharmacy.

The boy had escaped with one tin. He crouched beneath the front window, stabbing at its lid with a pocketknife. His hands were so weak he could scarcely force the blade through.

“Give it here,” the woman said.

He shook his head.

At six o’clock on an October morning in 1817, Captain Edward Vale discovered that the field chosen for his death was full of ordinary things.

A rook hopped along a broken fence. Somewhere beyond the mist, a farmer called to a dog. The grass had soaked through Edward’s boots while the seconds measured out the distance.

He had imagined, during the sleepless night, that the occasion would possess a certain grandeur. Instead, he felt cold and faintly foolish.

Across the field, Henry Ashcombe stood with his pistol lowered. Three evenings earlier, Edward had called him a liar before twelve gentlemen. Yesterday, a written apology might have settled it. Now there were carriages waiting beneath the trees, and men who had risen before dawn to witness satisfaction.

“Gentlemen,” said Ashcombe’s second.

Edward took his place.

At the signal, he raised his arm. He meant to fire above Ashcombe’s shoulder—not from generosity, exactly, but because killing a man over a sentence spoken after supper had begun to seem absurd.

The two reports came so close together that he heard only one.

Something struck him in the stomach with the blunt force of a fist. He sat down unexpectedly in the wet grass.

For a moment there was no pain.

Then he tried to stand.

His second, Charles Mercer, reached him before he fell sideways.

“Stay still, Ned.”

“I am quite all right.”

The pain arrived while he was saying it. His breath stopped halfway in. He bent forward, pressing both hands against his coat, and could not finish the reassuring smile he had begun.

The surgeon knelt beside him.

Edward watched the man’s expression change.

“No,” he said.

Nobody answered.

During the first minute, he was chiefly embarrassed. Ashcombe was approaching, and Edward wanted to meet him upright. He asked Charles to help him sit straighter, then cried out when they moved him.

During the second, he asked whether the carriage could be brought closer.

“We must get you warm,” Charles said.

“Then fetch it.”

But the surgeon kept one hand on Edward’s wrist and did not send anyone running.

By the third minute, the pain had become the only thing Edward could attend to. It rose whenever he breathed deeply and remained when he tried not to breathe at all. He gripped Charles’s sleeve and asked him to loosen his waistcoat. Once it was loose, he asked whether it might be fastened again.

Ashcombe knelt a few feet away.

“Vale, I never intended—”

“Don’t,” Edward said.

He had no strength for an apology, either to hear one or to give one.

The church clock began to strike six. They had started early.

Edward listened to each bell. Between the fourth and fifth, he remembered that his sister would be expecting him for breakfast. She had written to ask whether he preferred kidneys or eggs, a question he had not thought worth answering.

“Tell Eleanor I was coming.”

Charles bent close. “Of course.”

“No. Tell her I meant to come.”

In the fifth minute, he began asking for help without specifying what anyone should do. The surgeon gave instructions in a low voice. Charles held him. Ashcombe stood, took two aimless steps, and stopped.

Edward’s grip weakened, then tightened once more as another pain passed through him.

“Stay,” he whispered.

“I’m here, Ned.”

For a little while Charles continued saying it.

When the surgeon finally touched his shoulder, Charles looked up with an expression of irritation, as though he had been interrupted in the middle of something necessary.

Beyond the fence, the farmer called again. This time the dog came.

The case lay open on the table, its velvet compartments dark as missing teeth.

He removed each piece with the same economy of motion he used to button a shirt. Nothing clicked louder than it had to. Nothing touched the table except the folded cloth he had brought for that purpose. Under his hands, separate shapes became a single, spare machine.

In the adjoining apartment, someone was watching a game show. Applause rose through the wall, then faded.

He paused at a mark on the metal. He rubbed it with the cloth, held it beneath the lamp, and rubbed it again. When it was gone, he continued.

Across the square, workers were making the last adjustments to the stage. A woman in a red coat straightened a row of small flags. One kept tipping toward its neighbor. She corrected it twice before stepping back.

Minister Vale arrived behind schedule.

The crowd moved before the hitman saw him: faces turning, phones lifting, a brief compression around the barricades. Then Vale appeared beneath the white canopy, smiling as an aide spoke close to his ear. He touched the aide’s elbow, apparently reassuring him about something.

The hitman settled behind the rifle.

Through the scope, the square lost its clutter. The minister’s face stood apart from the flowers, the security detail, the huge printed promise hanging behind the lectern. He looked older than he had in the photograph. There was a small dressing near his jaw, probably a shaving cut.

The hitman made the final adjustment. The crosshairs came to rest on Vale’s head.

He felt no anger. He had read enough about the minister to recognize him and no more. The speeches, the allegations, the causes for which people praised or despised him—none had been necessary to the work.

Vale searched the front row. Finding someone, he smiled differently: less broadly, without showing his teeth. His hand lifted an inch from the lectern.

The hitman watched without curiosity.

Behind the wall, the game-show audience began applauding again. He waited for it to stop.

The motel towel had been white once. Now it lay beneath his thigh, soaked dark red in the middle, its frayed edges slowly turning pink.

He’d arranged everything on the nightstand: tweezers from a drugstore grooming kit, sewing scissors, a cracked hand mirror, half a bottle of vodka. Under the yellow bedside lamp, they looked less like tools than things someone had emptied from a lost suitcase.

He touched the wound and pain flashed all the way to his teeth.

“Okay,” he said, though nothing was.

Blood slicked his fingers. He wiped them on the bedspread and left four wavering streaks across the brown floral pattern. The air conditioner rattled in the window. Somewhere beyond the wall, a television audience laughed.

The bullet was still in there—or he thought it was. Every movement of his leg produced a deep, sick pressure, as though something had caught inside the muscle and refused to let go.

He picked up the tweezers. They clicked against the mirror because his hands were shaking.

The next attempt broke his breath into a strangled shout. His leg jerked before he could stop it, and a fresh wash of blood warmed the towel. For several seconds he could do nothing but grip the mattress, eyes squeezed shut, waiting for the pain to become something he could think around.

It didn’t. It stayed enormous.

When he opened his eyes, the tools were scattered on the carpet. He couldn’t remember dropping them.

He stared at the telephone beside the bed. Reaching for it meant moving. He sat there gathering himself for that small distance, then knocked the receiver loose with a bloody hand.

The photograph was placed on the table before the tools.

That was how Luca knew this would be worse than he had imagined.

His daughter stood outside her school, one shoe untied, laughing at something beyond the frame. He recognized the yellow sleeve of her coat. He had bought it in September.

Across from him, Moretti adjusted the photograph until its edges were parallel with the table.

“She looks like you.”

Luca kept his eyes on the picture. “She looks like her mother.”

“Yes,” Moretti said. “That was polite of me.”

Behind Luca, a chair scraped the floor. Someone sat down close enough that he could hear the man breathing.

For eleven months, Luca had carried two phones and answered to two names. In the mornings he had drunk coffee with men who trusted him. At night he had sat in a parked car beside a federal agent who called that trust *access*.

Neither word seemed adequate now.

Moretti set a recorder beside the photograph.

“I don’t need a confession. I need to know what they know.”

“I don’t know who you mean.”

Moretti sighed, not theatrically. The sigh of a man discovering that a delivery had arrived incomplete.

A hand closed around Luca’s wrist.

He pulled back before he could stop himself. The chair beneath him shifted an inch.

Moretti watched the movement.

“There,” he said. “You understand perfectly.”

The man behind Luca brought his hand onto the table and held it there. A small metal instrument clicked against the wood.

Luca looked at the door.

He had been doing that since they brought him in, measuring the distance automatically. Eight steps, perhaps six if he ran. Now he noticed that his coat hung from a hook beside it. Someone had taken the trouble to hang it up.

“Which finger do you write with?” Moretti asked.

“Wait.”

Moretti raised one finger. The pressure on Luca’s wrist eased slightly.

The relief was immediate and humiliating.

“Good,” Moretti said. “Tell me about Thursday.”

“Nothing happened Thursday.”

“Then Wednesday.”

“You’re making a mistake.”

Moretti lowered his finger.

Luca stared at his daughter’s photograph as the man behind him bent over his hand.

Then pain broke his concentration so completely that, for several seconds, there was no photograph, no room, no answer he could give. He heard himself cry out. He tried to stand, but the man’s weight kept him in the chair.

When he could see the table clearly again, a folded cloth covered the finger where the nail had been.

He could not make himself look beneath it.

The pain kept surging. He waited for each wave to diminish, only to discover how little it diminished before the next. His breathing sounded strange to him—quick, shallow, interrupted by small involuntary noises he could not suppress.

Moretti poured water into a glass.

“Thursday,” he said.

Luca tried to swallow. His mouth would not cooperate.

“The garage.”

“Which garage?”

“Bell Street.”

Moretti moved the glass closer, but not close enough for Luca to reach with his free hand.

“Who was there?”

A name came to him. His handler’s name.

He had practiced withholding it through sleepless nights, had imagined being brave or clever, had prepared lies inside other lies. Now he could barely hold the name in his mind without speaking it.

“I need a minute.”

Moretti glanced at his watch.

“All right.”

He waited.

That was worse than the question. The quiet gave Luca time to feel his hand, to hear the instrument being set down and picked up again. He watched Moretti’s face for impatience and found none.

At last, Luca gave him the name.

Moretti slid the water within reach.

“And now,” he said gently, “tell me which of your other answers we need to revisit.”

The city called him a sanitation specialist. The men who paid him called him a cleaner. His daughter, when she still called, told people he worked in recycling.

At two in the morning, a van reversed into Bay Four.

Marek watched it on the security monitor while stirring powdered milk into his coffee. The camera had a dead pixel in the center of the loading dock. Anyone who stepped there acquired a small white star on their chest.

Tonight there were two men and a sealed transport cradle.

One man wore an expensive coat. The other wore disposable gloves.

“Priority,” said the coat.

Marek slid the intake tablet across the counter.

“Everything’s priority.”

The man signed with a false name. Marek didn’t look at it. Names made no difference to the machinery, and he had spent years trying to arrange the rest of his life on the same principle.

Beyond the counter stood six industrial vats behind opaque shielding. Pipes climbed from them into a filtration system that occupied most of the ceiling. A municipal permit hung beside the door, authorizing the reclamation of contaminated biological material.

It was a real permit. In this city, the expensive part of a lie was making it official.

The man in gloves helped move the cradle onto the transfer rail. Its cover had pulled loose at one corner.

A bare foot showed.

Marek stopped stirring his coffee.

There was a small adhesive star on the heel, the sort children put on everything they owned and half the things they didn’t.

He pulled the cover straight.

“Anything else?” he asked.

The coat shook his head. Both men left before the bay door had finished opening.

Marek waited for it to close again. Then he logged the delivery as spoiled tissue from an unlicensed clinic.

The automated rig took over. It drew the cradle through the shielded doorway and lowered its contents into one of the chemical baths. Marek could see none of this directly. On his console, a diagram changed color. Pumps started overhead, followed by the deep, uneven vibration of the extraction system.

He had once watched through a maintenance viewer.

Only once. He had wanted to know exactly what he was doing. For several months afterward, he had been unable to eat soup.

Now he kept his eyes on the gauges. The vats were old, their automated systems patched with parts intended for other machines. If something failed, it would be Marek standing beside it, not the men in coats.

He checked the seals, acknowledged a pressure warning, and called up the maintenance history. Vat Three needed servicing again. He submitted a request he knew would be deferred.

Behind the barrier, the bath continued its work.

His first year, he had counted the people.

His second year, he had counted the payments.

Lately he counted the steps between the console and the vending machine. Twenty-three going there. Twenty-four coming back if he stopped at the waste bin.

He bought a packet of crackers. They had been manufactured to look toasted, each one printed with a slightly different arrangement of brown spots.

His wrist terminal vibrated.

A message from his daughter:

**Found an apartment. Smaller than the pictures. You’d hate the stairs.**

Below it was a photograph of a narrow room with a mattress on the floor. Rain gleamed on the window. A plant stood in a chipped mug.

Marek enlarged the picture until the mug filled the screen.

He knew it. Blue glaze, broken handle. She had taken it when she moved out, though he remembered insisting she leave it behind because it belonged to a set.

He typed:

**Looks nice.**

He deleted that.

**Do you need money?**

He deleted that too. She had asked him to stop asking.

The console chimed. He lowered his wrist and returned to work.

There were further stages after the bath, all enclosed, all given harmless names on the display. Treatment. Recovery. Transfer. What came out passed into sealed waste systems under another company’s license. Marek’s job was to supervise, record, and leave nothing in the receiving bay that might interest the morning staff.

He wiped the transfer rail. He cleaned the cradle and set it on the return rack. One of its wheels squeaked, so he marked it defective.

Near the drain, he found the adhesive star.

It must have fallen when he straightened the cover.

He crouched with a cloth in his hand. The star was yellow, one point folded underneath. For a moment he tried to decide whether picking it up required fresh gloves.

Then he sat down on the edge of the empty cradle.

He waited.

Years ago, he would have known what to expect: nausea, trembling, a need to get outside. Sometimes he had cried in his car without understanding why that particular night had done it.

Now there was only the hum of the room and a stiff ache in his knees.

He looked at the star and felt nothing he could name. Not even relief at feeling nothing.

His wrist terminal lit again.

**You can visit, you know.**

Marek read the message twice.

He pictured himself in the little room, sitting on the mattress because there was nowhere else. His daughter would make coffee. He would complain about the stairs. She might laugh, or she might remember that he had always found something wrong with wherever she lived.

He didn’t know how to arrive without bringing this place with him.

The vats fell quiet.

Marek picked up the star with the cloth and put both in the waste bin. He washed his hands, although the gloves had stayed intact. Then he sat at the console and opened his daughter’s message.

**Saturday?** he typed.

He sent it before he could replace it with something easier.

On the security monitor, headlights turned into the loading dock.

Marek set his wrist terminal facedown and went to open the bay.

“He saw us.”

“I heard you the first time.”

“Then stop looking at the clock.”

“I’m looking at the clock because we’re late.”

Marek stood beside the office door, one hand resting on the knob. Through the frosted glass, the hostage was a pale shape in a chair.

“He called me by my name,” Marek said.

“You told him your name.”

“I told *you* my name. He was supposed to be on the floor.”

“Well. Add it to his list of offenses.”

Marek turned. “You think this is funny?”

“No,” Vale said. “I think you’re embarrassed, and you want to make that his problem.”

For a moment, the only sound was the fluorescent tube above them.

“He gives them our faces, we’re finished.”

“Maybe.”

“He gives them my name—”

“It’s a common name.”

“Not with this face.”

Vale glanced at him. “There’s the tragedy.”

Marek’s hand tightened on the knob.

“Move away from the door,” Vale said.

“You giving orders now?”

“I’ve been giving orders all morning. You stopped liking them when something went wrong.”

“We agreed. No loose ends.”

“We agreed to rob a bank. You keep trying to improve the arrangement.”

The chair scraped on the other side of the glass. Both men went quiet.

Then Marek said, more softly, “He’s listening.”

“He’s been listening the whole time.”

“So he knows what we’re discussing.”

“Yes.”

“And you expect him to forget?”

“I expect him to want to go home.”

“That isn’t enough.”

“It was enough for you ten minutes ago.”

Marek looked down at the bags by Vale’s feet.

“Don’t do that,” Vale said.

“Do what?”

“Count your share while you decide.”

“I’m thinking.”

“No. You’ve decided. You’re waiting for me to say it so you can remember it differently.”

Marek took his hand off the knob.

“You’d let me carry it?”

“You brought it up.”

“We’re partners.”

“Then ask me.”

Marek stared at him.

“Ask,” Vale repeated.

“Will you help me?”

“No.”

The answer seemed to leave less air in the room.

“Since when have you had principles?” Marek asked.

Vale picked up the bags. “I have preferences.”

“And if he talks?”

“Then we’ll both wish he hadn’t.”

Marek stayed by the door.

Vale waited, impatient now.

At last Marek stepped away.

From inside the office came a muffled, breathless “Thank you.”

Marek stopped.

“Keep walking,” Vale said.
